docs.title: MIMIQ TensorWeaver
docs.text:
A Matrix Product State (MPS) quantum circuit simulator for MIMIQ.

part of MIMIQ, by

TensorWeaver simulates quantum circuits by representing the state as a Matrix Product State rather than a dense state vector. The bond dimension χ is a single controllable trade-off between accuracy and cost: circuits with limited entanglement run well past the reach of state-vector simulation, and you decide how much approximation to accept.

It plugs into MIMIQ. You build circuits with mimiqcircuits, run them with tensorweaver.execute, and receive the same QCSResults object MIMIQ uses elsewhere.

New to tensor networks? Start with Concepts, which explains MPS, bond dimension, and truncation from the beginning.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX, BitString
from tensorweaver import execute

# A Bell-state circuit.
c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=1000, bonddim=64)
print(results.histogram())                      # {bs"00": 511, bs"11": 489}
print(f"Fidelity: {results.fidelities[0]:.6f}")

# Ask for specific amplitudes.
bs00, bs11 = BitString([0, 0]), BitString([1, 1])
results = execute(c, nsamples=100, bonddim=64, bitstrings=[bs00, bs11])
print(f"⟨00|ψ⟩ = {results.amplitudes[bs00]}")
print(f"⟨11|ψ⟩ = {results.amplitudes[bs11]}")

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Matrix Product State core written in Rust, exposed through PyO3.
  • MIMIQ circuits decomposed automatically to TensorWeaver's native gate set.
  • Multi-controlled gates applied directly, without a CX decomposition.
  • Mid-circuit measurement, reset, and classically conditioned operations.
  • Noise simulation via Kraus and mixed-unitary channels, sampled as trajectories.
  • Observables read from the state: amplitudes, expectation values, bond dimension, Schmidt rank, entanglement entropy.
  • Qubit reordering to lower the bond dimension of long-range circuits.
  • Qudits: sites of any physical dimension d ≥ 2 on the low-level MPS/MPO API.
  • Three linear-algebra engines selectable per simulator at runtime with linalg: OpenBLAS (vendored), Intel MKL and pure-Rust faer. Left unset it takes the preferred engine the wheel for this platform carries.
  • Qiskit interoperability through an optional extra.
  • Results returned as MIMIQ QCSResults: samples, amplitudes, fidelities, timings.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
An index of the public surface. For what the knobs mean see Concepts, for execute()'s keywords see Circuit Execution, and for runnable code see Examples.

Gate and operator matrix inputs

Anything taking a one- or two-qubit gate or operator (apply_gate_1q, apply_gate_2q, expectation_1q, expectation_2q, apply_kraus_*) accepts a numpy array of dtype complex128: (2, 2) for a 1Q gate, (4, 4) for a 2Q gate, (n_ops, dim, dim) for a stack of Kraus operators. On a qudit site of dimension d, the shapes are (d, d) and (d₁·d₂, d₁·d₂).

A flat list of floats in column-major [re, im, re, im, ...] order is also accepted, with length 8 for a 1Q gate and 32 for a 2Q gate. It is deprecated; use numpy arrays.

Bitstring / qubit ordering

TensorWeaver is little-endian by qubit index: bitstring position i is qubit i. This is the opposite of Qiskit's convention, so bitstrings from mps.sample_bitstring(), mps.sample(), results.cstates, and results.histogram() appear reversed compared to Qiskit output. The same applies to the bitstring argument of mps.amplitude().

docs.title: tensorweaver.execute(circuit, nsamples=..., *, num_qubits=..., bonddim=..., entdim=..., max_bond_dim=..., sv_cutoff=..., algorithm=..., post_compress=..., strict_bonddim=..., seed=..., bitstrings=..., reorderqubits=..., fuse=..., fuse_threshold=..., canonicaldecompose=..., simplify=..., buffer=..., traversal=..., linalg=..., usegpu=..., usemkl=...)
TwSimulator
docs.text:
A reusable simulator. Configuration is fixed at construction; nsamples, seed, and num_qubits are per call.

Bases: LocalBackend

MPS quantum circuit simulator, backed by the TensorWeaver core.

Subclasses :class:mimiqcircuits.backends.LocalBackend, so the usual sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=..., seed=...) call works and returns a :class:mimiqcircuits.QCSResults. :meth:capabilities lists what it can serve.

Every knob below is set on the constructor and fixed for the life of the instance; build a new simulator to change one. Accepting them per call as well would mean distinguishing "not passed" from "passed the default" on every keyword.

Execution mode. The circuit decides, not a keyword. Trailing measurements are split off into a classical projection and do not count. If everything left is unitary, the state is evolved once and nsamples bitstrings are drawn from it (sampling mode, one entry in results.fidelities). If any surviving operation on qubits is non-unitary (a mid-circuit Measure or Reset, a noise channel, qubit loss), the circuit is re-evolved from scratch nsamples times (trajectory mode, one fidelity and one cstate per trajectory).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bonddim int

Maximum MPS bond dimension, the memory and accuracy knob. Default 256. Raising it lets the state carry more entanglement before truncation, at a cost that grows steeply; lowering it truncates earlier and lowers the reported fidelity.

256 entdim int

Maximum bond dimension of the MPO that gates are fused into between state updates. Default 16. Larger values batch more gates per update. A gate whose operator rank exceeds entdim raises rather than being applied at reduced accuracy, so raise entdim if a circuit reports that.

16 sv_cutoff float | None

Singular-value floor applied when an MPO is compressed into the state. None (default) uses the library default 1e-7. Lower it toward machine precision for accuracy, raise it for speed.

None mpo_cutoff float | None

Singular-value floor applied while gates are fused into the MPO. None (default) uses the library default 1e-15, which is essentially exact. Independent of sv_cutoff; there is rarely a reason to change it.

None algorithm Algorithm

How each fused MPO is applied to the state. The names read as the method plus what it applies: "dmpo" is direct MPO application, "cmpo" canonical, and "vmpoa" / "vmpob" variational variants a and b. "vmpoa" (default) and "vmpob" run single- and two-site variational sweeps seeded by a zip-up. The default matches MPSSim's (MPO1z), so results are comparable with the incumbent MIMIQ engine without tuning. "dmpo" is the zip-up alone, the cheapest per application.

"cmpo" is a single pass like "dmpo", arranged so the weight it discards is chosen against the state's own Schmidt spectrum. Where the ceiling binds it keeps more of the state and tends to leave it narrower, which makes later gates cheaper too, at close to single-pass cost. It is also the accurate choice under usegpu=True. See the "Choosing an algorithm" page of the manual for how to decide.

'vmpoa' strict_bonddim bool | None

Whether every intermediate bond must stay within bonddim while an MPO is applied. It never changes the bond dimension of the result, which is at most bonddim either way.

  • None (default): the algorithm's own default, strict for "dmpo", "vmpoa" and "vmpob", relaxed for "cmpo".
  • True, strict: the zip-up ("dmpo", and the seed of the two variational algorithms) cuts its carry to bonddim as it goes, so the memory a run needs follows from bonddim alone. Those cuts are made in a gauge where the singular values are not the state's Schmidt values, so they can drop weight the result did not need to lose. At bonddim < entdim (fused MPOs reach bond dimension entdim) a cut can wipe out the state altogether, so a strict run needs bonddim >= entdim. From there up, "dmpo" suffers most, above all with post_compress=False; the variational sweeps repair most of it. The reported fidelity shows the loss: a strict run is less accurate, not silently wrong.
  • False, relaxed: the zip-up's carry may grow to max(4 * bonddim, D) for an MPO of bond dimension D and is cut to bonddim afterwards, in canonical form. The result is exact whenever it fits under bonddim, and entdim may be anything, at the price of more memory and 1.5 to 4 times the time. For the variational algorithms, it seeds the sweeps from this relaxed zip-up: on 20-qubit random circuits "vmpoa" reached 5 to 15% lower infidelity than strict, and "vmpob" matched strict, at 1.4 to 4 times the time.

"cmpo" has no strict form, so algorithm="cmpo" with strict_bonddim=True raises :class:ValueError here. A run that resolves to strict (True, or None with "dmpo", "vmpoa" or "vmpob") with bonddim < entdim also raises :class:ValueError here, before any circuit runs: raise bonddim to entdim or above, lower entdim, or pass strict_bonddim=False. A value that is neither a bool nor None raises :class:TypeError. Applies on host and device.

None post_compress bool

Run the global recond and compression sweep after every MPO application. Default True. The sweep restores canonical form, which is what keeps the next zip-up's singular values equal to the physical Schmidt weights. Turning it off defers one sweep to end of circuit: faster on circuits that stay well below bonddim, but bond dimension then creeps on zip-up noise until the zipper's intermediate, which carries the MPO bond index and not the state's, crosses bonddim, and truncation in the wrong gauge corrupts the state. Measured on a 16-qubit QFT at bonddim=64: mirror fidelity 1.0 with it on, 0.535 with it off, and the reported fidelity reads 1.0 either way.

True seed int | None

Master RNG seed for every run this instance drives. None (default) draws fresh entropy per run. A seed= on :meth:execute overrides it.

None buffer int

Depth of the gate-fusion pipeline. 0 (default) fuses and applies inline; a positive value runs fusion on a background thread that prepares up to buffer MPOs ahead while evolution applies them, overlapping the fusion of the next block with the application of the current one. Results are identical to buffer=0. The overlap is real parallelism because mps.apply_mpo releases the GIL, and a depth of 2 to 4 is enough because only one or two MPOs are ever in flight.

0 traversal Traversal

Order in which gates are walked while they are fused into MPOs. "sequential" (default) is the circuit's insertion order; "bfs" is a breadth-first topological order that groups mutually independent gates into layers; "dfs" is depth-first, following one dependency chain to its end before backtracking. All three produce the same simulated state and differ only in how gates batch into MPOs, which shifts the intermediate bond dimension and therefore the runtime. "bfs" tends to pack each MPO with more commuting gates, which helps on wide, shallow layers.

'sequential' linalg Linalg | None

Linear-algebra library: "openblas", "mkl" or "faer". None (default) takes whichever engine this build ships, preferring OpenBLAS: it is vendored into the wheel, so it works from a plain pip install. Where the wheel has no OpenBLAS engine, which is the Windows wheel, the default resolves to MKL instead. "mkl" is Intel MKL, whose runtime the wheel cannot bundle and must come from the environment; if it is absent, the first use raises :class:ImportError with installation instructions. "faer" is a pure-Rust library with no system dependency, usually slower than the other two. A named engine the build does not have raises at first use rather than switching engine. An unknown name raises :class:ValueError. The resolved value is readable as sim.linalg.

None usegpu bool

Run the state on an NVIDIA GPU. False by default. The whole MPS is moved into device memory once, evolved there, and moved back once, so a circuit pays one transfer at each end rather than one per gate. Requires algorithm="dmpo" or "cmpo", the two single-pass algorithms with a device implementation. The CUDA engine is one module whose host provider is OpenBLAS, so linalg must be unset or "openblas"; any other value raises :class:ValueError. Raises :class:ImportError at first use if this build has no CUDA engine or no GPU is reachable. Prefer "cmpo", the accurate one of the two.

Whether it is faster depends on the bond dimension. The device wins where the state is large and loses where it is small, because each site's truncated SVD carries a fixed launch cost that the host does not pay. Measured on an A30 against one Xeon core, on a 24-qubit brick-layer circuit: 0.8× at bonddim=64, 2.8× at 128, 8.2× at 256, 24× at 512. So below roughly 64 the GPU is slower, and the case for it grows with the problem. Both paths truncate identically, and the reported fidelities agree to every digit.

False max_num_threads int | None

The most threads a run of this simulator uses, for the linear algebra and for sampling alike. None (default) leaves both to the process setting (see :func:thread_info). The cap is held for the length of each :meth:execute, :meth:evolve, :meth:evolvezerostate and :meth:expectation call and released after, so it never outlives the run. The thread counts are process-wide: simulators running at the same time on different Python threads share them, and each runs at the smallest cap any of them holds. Raises :class:ValueError below 1.

None usemkl bool | None

Deprecated, use linalg. True means linalg="mkl" and False means linalg="openblas". Passing it emits a :class:DeprecationWarning, and passing it with a linalg that names a different engine raises :class:ValueError.

None

Reordering under traversal applies only to the fusable gates between state-reading or measuring instructions. Measurement, reset, channel, observable (Amplitude / BondDim / SchmidtRank / ExpectationValue), barrier and IfStatement stay put and act as synchronisation points. Within a gate run, two gates are ordered relative to each other only when they share a qubit.

Which engines a wheel carries depends on the platform, because the compute core binds the CBLAS and LAPACKE interfaces directly and no one provider supplies both everywhere: Linux x86-64 ships OpenBLAS, MKL and faer, macOS arm64 OpenBLAS and faer (MKL is x86-only), Windows x86-64 MKL and faer. faer is pure Rust and binds neither interface. This is why linalg defaults to None rather than to an engine name.

Each engine is a separate native module, so linalg and usegpu are per instance and simulators on different engines can run side by side in one process. Their objects do not interoperate: an :class:~tensorweaver.MPS, :class:~tensorweaver.MPO, Rng or :class:~tensorweaver.TwState built by one engine cannot be passed to a simulator or method using the other, which raises TypeError. To carry a state across engines, round-trip it through MPS.serialize() and MPS.deserialize(), which copies it.

Caveats

  • num_qubits= on :meth:execute is a TensorWeaver-specific kwarg (also accepted by :class:quantanium.QuantaniumQCS); :class:mimiqengines.MPSSimulator does not expose it. Code that drives the three simulators with a portable sim.execute(c, nsamples=100, seed=42) shape is unaffected.
  • Amplitudes requested in trajectory mode reflect the last shot's state, not an ensemble average, whenever the circuit contains a mid-circuit measure, reset or IfStatement.
  • RNG resolution priority: a call-site seed= beats the instance seed, which beats fresh entropy from :mod:secrets. The free function tensorweaver.execute(...) defaults to seed=42; this method resolves to a concrete int before forwarding, so the two surfaces never collide.
  • :meth:bind substitutes parameters and re-runs the full compile pipeline; there is no native parametric fast path.
  • :meth:evolve returns (state, TruncationLowerBound) and never promotes to ExactFidelity even when fid == 1.0, because each MPO application is an SVD truncation event whose fidelity is at best a lower bound.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorweaver import TwSimulator
>>> sim = TwSimulator(bonddim=64)
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
...
>>> c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
...
>>> c.push(mc.Measure(), [0, 1], [0, 1])
...
>>> results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=100, seed=42)

Long-range gates cost more bond dimension than neighbouring ones, but no routing or SWAP insertion is required of the caller.

docs.title: build_state(nq, nb=0, nz=0, **_)
docs.text:
Allocate a fresh |0…0⟩ state on nq qubits.

The MPS is capped at this simulator's bonddim and built on this simulator's engine, so it can only be used with this simulator. nb and nz size the classical-bit and complex registers.

docs.title: zerostate(nq, nb=0, nz=0)
docs.text: Back-compat alias for :meth:build_state.

docs.title: evolvezerostate(circuit, *, seed=None)
docs.text:
Evolve a fresh zero state through circuit and return it.

Returns (state, fidelity), the fidelity being a plain float lower bound on the evolved state. This is a single evolution, so a circuit with mid-circuit measurement or noise gives one trajectory, not an ensemble; use :meth:execute for that.

Seed resolution: call-site seed=, then the instance seed, then fresh cryptographic entropy from :mod:secrets.

docs.title: compile(circuit)
docs.text:
Lower circuit for the MPS evolution loop.

Populates :attr:CompileMetadata.active_qubits. Decomposition to TensorWeaverBasis and fusion into MPOs happen later, in :meth:evolve. Qubit reordering is not done here: it is a pass, which :meth:execute runs before compiling when asked to (see :meth:reorder_pass).

docs.title: default_passes()
docs.text: No passes run by default, so a circuit runs as written.

docs.title: reorder_pass(method=None, *, seed=None)
docs.text:
The pass execute(reorderqubits=...) adds.

A :class:~tensorweaver.TwReorderQubitsPass scored against this simulator's bonddim. method=None, which is what reorderqubits=True asks for, runs the whole search portfolio; a method name pins one search. To set the pass's alpha or margin, build it yourself and pass it through passes=.

docs.title: simplify_pass()
docs.text:
The pass execute(simplify=True) adds.

A :class:~mimiqcircuits.SimplifyPass running :data:~mimiqcircuits.DEFAULT_SIMPLIFY_PASSES without resynthesize_2q. That pass rewrites every two-qubit block, which reorders the gates and makes the MPS evolution slower even when it saves a CX. To run it anyway, pass a SimplifyPass through passes=.

docs.title: expectation(state, op, *qubits)
docs.text:
Compute ⟨ψ|op|ψ⟩ on state without mutating it.

Exact, with no sampling involved. Supports 1- and 2-qubit operators and a :class:PauliString of any length. qubits are the 0-based indices op acts on, in the operator's own leg order, and there must be exactly as many as the operator has qubits.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

if the qubit count does not match the operator, or if a dense operator acts on three or more qubits.

docs.title: evolve(state, compiled, *, rng=None, callback=None, stopped=None)
docs.text:
Evolve state under compiled, in place.

Returns (state, TruncationLowerBound). The product of the per-step fidelities is always wrapped as :class:TruncationLowerBound, never collapsed to :class:ExactFidelity even at fid == 1.0, because that scalar bounds the fidelity from below rather than claiming the exact state was reproduced.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if compiled is not a :class:CompiledCircuit.

docs.title: apply_segment(state, insts, *, rng=None)
docs.text:
Fuse a run of loss-free instructions into MPOs and apply it.

Returns the truncation fidelity of the run. Every qubit in the run is present, so fusing it cannot bury an operation a fired loss should have dropped. The run is padded to the register width, so one that misses the high qubits still builds full-width MPOs.

docs.title: apply_instruction(state, inst, *, rng=None)
docs.text:
Apply a single instruction the driver issues around a loss boundary.

These are a reload Reset, a Check or MeasureCheck SetBit, or a partial-loss rewrite. A multi-qubit gate has to be fused into an MPO, so it is routed through :meth:apply_segment; everything else applies directly to the MPS.

docs.title: sample_kraus(state, channel, targets, *, rng=None)
docs.text:
Sample one branch of a Kraus channel against the live state and apply it.

Returns (fidelity, fired_operator). The operator returned is the original one, not a reconstruction, so a LossyOperator branch reaches the driver with its tag intact.

docs.title: execute(circuit, *, nsamples=1000, seed=None, rng=None, num_qubits=None, passes=None, fuse=None, fuse_threshold=None, canonicaldecompose=None, reorderqubits=None, remove_swaps=None, simplify=None, reorderqubits_seed=None, callback=None, param_grid=None, strict_pass_order=True, stopped=None, progress=False)
docs.text:
Execute circuit and return :class:QCSResults.

The TensorWeaver configuration (bonddim, entdim, sv_cutoff, mpo_cutoff, algorithm, strict_bonddim, post_compress, buffer, traversal, linalg, usegpu) comes from the constructor, not from this call. Circuit preparation, qubit reordering included, comes from this call. Amplitudes and expectation values are requested by putting :class:Amplitude and :class:ExpectationValue operations in the circuit; they write into results.zstates.

Whether the run is a single evolution plus nsamples draws, or nsamples independent trajectories, follows from the circuit; see the class docstring.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default circuit Circuit | SweepExperiment | list

One circuit, a list of circuits to run in turn, or a :class:~mimiqcircuits.SweepExperiment, which runs its circuit once per point of its parameter table, as param_grid does.

required nsamples int

Bitstrings to draw in sampling mode, or trajectories to run in trajectory mode. Default 1000.

1000 seed int | None

Master RNG seed for this run. Overrides the instance seed. Mutually exclusive with rng.

None rng Random | None

A :class:random.Random to draw the run's seeds from. Mutually exclusive with seed.

None num_qubits int | None

Width of the simulated register. None (default) infers it from the circuit. This keyword is TensorWeaver-specific.

None passes PassPipeline | None

Extra circuit-preparation passes, appended after the ones the flags below select, as given.

None fuse bool | None

Fuse runs of gates into GateCustom blocks before evolution (the client-side FusePass). Default None, which does not fuse. This is distinct from, and usually redundant with, the MPO fusion this simulator does internally while evolving.

None fuse_threshold int | None

Minimum qubit count for fuse to act. Default None. On its own it asks to fuse; with fuse=False it raises ValueError.

None canonicaldecompose bool | None

Decompose to the canonical basis before evolution. Default None, which does not decompose.

None reorderqubits bool | str | None

Relabel the qubits before evolution to bring interacting ones closer together, which lowers bond-dimension growth. None (default) and False leave the layout alone. True runs the whole portfolio of layout searches and keeps the best one scored against bonddim, or the circuit's own layout when none clearly beats it. A method name ("greedy", "sa", "multilevel") pins one search. The pass is :meth:reorder_pass; to tune its alpha or margin, pass a :class:~tensorweaver.TwReorderQubitsPass through passes= instead. Results come back in your qubit numbering, and the search report lands in :attr:last_layout_report.

None remove_swaps bool | None

Server-side only: raises when set locally.

None simplify bool | None

Simplify the circuit before evolution with :class:~mimiqcircuits.SimplifyPass, which cancels inverse pairs, merges rotations and resynthesizes one-qubit blocks while keeping the unitary exactly (see :meth:simplify_pass). Default None, which does not simplify. It runs before fuse and reorderqubits, so those see the shorter circuit. To pick the simplification passes, pass a SimplifyPass through passes= instead.

None reorderqubits_seed int | None

Seed for the layout search alone. None (default) draws it from the run's RNG. On its own it does not ask for reordering.

None callback object | None

Called as callback(applied, total) as the evolution progresses. total is None because MPOs are fused lazily and the count is not known up front.

None param_grid list[dict] | None

List of parameter dicts. Each is substituted into the circuit and executed with its own derived seed, and the return value becomes a list of results, one per grid point. A SweepExperiment does the same and checks that its table binds every free symbol of the circuit; pass one or the other.

None strict_pass_order bool

Enforce the pass pipeline's declared ordering constraints. Default True.

True stopped object | None

Cooperative cancellation handle checked during evolution.

None progress bool

Show a progress display. Default False.

False

docs.title: TwDirectSimulator
docs.text:
A simulator that applies a circuit one operation at a time and builds no MPO. Distant qubits are swapped next to each other and stay where they were moved; every read-out answers in your qubit numbering.

Bases: TwSimulator

MPS simulator that applies a circuit one operation at a time.

Where :class:~tensorweaver.TwSimulator fuses gates into matrix product operators and applies each one in a sweep, this simulator builds no MPO. Each gate updates the state directly:

  • a one-qubit gate acts on the site of its qubit;
  • a two-qubit gate acts on two neighbouring sites, contracted together and split back with one truncated SVD. Qubits that are not neighbours are first brought together with swaps of adjacent sites. Which of the two moves is routing's choice: by default the one that leaves the next gates closer, where its swaps cannot truncate, and otherwise the gate's second qubit, next to its first (for a CX, the target to the control);
  • a gate on three to max_gate_qubits qubits gathers them into one block of sites and acts there in one step. A larger gate is decomposed.

Qubits move and stay moved. Routing swaps are not undone. The state keeps track of where each qubit sits, so a second gate on the same pair needs no routing, and every read-out (sampling, measurement, amplitudes, expectation values) answers in your qubit numbering. :meth:evolvezerostate sorts the chain back at the end and returns the plain MPS, with qubit i on site i. :meth:execute skips that sort, since nothing it reads needs it.

Fidelity. Every swap is a truncated SVD at sv_cutoff and bonddim, like a gate, and what it discards is in the reported fidelity.

Not supported. BondDim, SchmidtRank and VonNeumannEntropy read a bond of the chain, and the chain is in whatever order routing left it, so circuits containing them are refused, as are noise channels on three or more qubits. There is no GPU path.

Which to use. This simulator pays one SVD per two-qubit gate, plus the routing swaps. :class:~tensorweaver.TwSimulator pays one sweep per fused block of gates. Circuits of local gates, or with few gates per qubit between read-outs, favour this one; deep, dense circuits at large bonddim favour MPO fusion.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bonddim int

Maximum MPS bond dimension. Default 256.

256 sv_cutoff float | None

Singular values below this are discarded by every gate and swap. None (default) uses the library default, 1e-7.

None max_gate_qubits int

The most qubits a gate may act on before it is decomposed. Default 4.

DEFAULT_MAX_GATE_QUBITS routing Routing

Which qubit a two-qubit gate moves. "lookahead" (default) moves either one: whichever leaves the next 16 two-qubit gates closer, as long as every bond its swaps cross is at most half of bonddim, so that no swap can truncate. Elsewhere it moves the gate's second qubit next to its first. "target" always does that: for a CX, the target to the control. On the MQT Bench u3+cx circuits at 100 qubits the lookahead was 1.1 to 3.6x faster on 11 of 13 inputs, and up to 1.4x slower on the other two (transpiled qft and qftentangled). It is applied by this package, not the engine.

'lookahead' seed int | None

Default master seed for :meth:execute. None (default) draws fresh entropy per run.

None linalg Linalg | None

Linear-algebra library, "openblas", "mkl" or "faer", as for :class:~tensorweaver.TwSimulator. None (default) takes the preferred engine this build ships.

None max_num_threads int | None

The most threads a run uses, as for :class:~tensorweaver.TwSimulator. None (default) leaves it to the process setting.

None usemkl bool | None

Deprecated, use linalg, as for :class:~tensorweaver.TwSimulator.

None

Example::

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorweaver import TwDirectSimulator

c = mc.Circuit()
c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
# Qubits 0 and 9 are far apart on the chain: qubit 9 is swapped down
# next to qubit 0, and stays there for the next gate.
c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 9)
c.push(mc.GateCZ(), 9, 0)
c.push(mc.Measure(), range(10), range(10))

sim = TwDirectSimulator(bonddim=64)
results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=1)
print(results.histogram())

docs.text:
Bases: DecompositionBasis

Decomposition basis targeting TensorWeaver's native gate set.

Terminal operations, executed directly by TensorWeaver: - 1Q parametric: GateRX, GateRY, GateRZ, GateU - 1Q identity: GateID, skipped during execution - 2Q optimized: GateCX, GateCZ, GateISWAP - 2Q generic: any 2-qubit unitary gate, fused into an MPO from its matrix - Multi-controlled: Control(n, 1Q-gate), any number of controls - Measurement/reset: Measure, Reset, MeasureReset - Conditional: IfStatement, terminal when its inner operation is - Z-variable ops: Amplitude, BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy, ExpectationValue, all of which observe the state without changing it - Classical: AbstractClassical logic (Not, And, Or, Xor, SetBit0/SetBit1) and the z-register arithmetic Add, Multiply, Pow - Noise channels: any krauschannel subclass, Kraus or mixed unitary - Scheduling: Barrier, a gate-fusion boundary with no effect on the state - Annotations: AbstractAnnotation, which carries no simulation semantics

Anything else is decomposed through the canonical rewrite rule, which delegates to each gate's _decompose(). A gate that neither is terminal nor decomposes raises :class:DecompositionError.

Example

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateCCX, GateH from mimiqcircuits.decomposition import decompose from tensorweaver.basis import TensorWeaverBasis c = Circuit() c.push(GateH(), 0) 1-qubit circuit with 1 instruction: └── H @ q[0] c.push(GateCCX(), 0, 1, 2) 3-qubit circuit with 2 instructions: ├── H @ q[0] └── C₂X @ q[0:1], q[2] decomposed = decompose(c, TensorWeaverBasis())

docs.title: TwReorderQubitsPass
docs.text:
The qubit-reordering pass that execute(reorderqubits=...) runs. Build it yourself and pass it through passes= to set its options; see Qubit ordering.

Bases: AbstractPass

Reorder qubits to reduce MPS bond-dimension growth.

An MPS lays the qubits out on a line, so a gate between two distant qubits pushes entanglement through every site between them. This pass relabels the qubits with a permutation π chosen by the native choose_layout (whose result does not depend on the engine).

Searches minimise the weighted-distance cost Cα(π) = Σ |π(i) − π(j)|^α · w(i, j), which is smooth and cheap to update. What picks between their results is a different cost, one that knows the bond dimension the run will use: per bond, how many truncations happen there times how many bits each one has to discard against it. The circuit's own layout is always a candidate, so a search that finds nothing better leaves it alone. The rewritten circuit is equivalent to the original; the pipeline maps the results back to the user's qubit frame.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: method: None (default) runs the whole portfolio and keeps whichever result scores best. A single spelling ("greedy", "sa" / "simulated_annealing", "multilevel", or True for "greedy") pins one search, which is still scored the same way. alpha: Exponent in the distance the search minimises. None (default) sweeps it, since every result is scored afterwards and a pointless exponent simply loses. Only 1.0 has a meaning: there the sum is identically the number of bond truncations the layout causes. seed: Seed for the stochastic searches. None (default) draws one from the pass-context RNG. bonddim: The bond dimension the run will use, which is what makes the cost meaningful. None (default) reads it off the backend in the pass context, falling back to 256 when the context has none. margin: How much better than the circuit's own layout a candidate must score before it is applied. A layout that truncates nothing is applied whatever the margin.

docs.title: See also

MockTensorWeaver and MockTwSimulator are the same class, and MockState is the state it returns. See Without a licence.

Bases: TwSimulator

TensorWeaver's LocalBackend interface, with no simulation behind it.

Same constructor as :class:~tensorweaver.TwSimulator, same execute, same :meth:capabilities, same :meth:limits, same :meth:topology, same refusals. Results are real :class:~mimiqcircuits.QCSResults objects built by the shared LocalBackend driver and carrying all-zero samples, zero amplitudes and expectation values, and fidelity 1.0.

What it is for: exercising the MIMIQ data models end to end (circuit in, passes, compilation, the sampling and trajectory routing, QCSResults, BitString, the protobuf round-trip) on a machine with no licence. It is not an approximation of TensorWeaver; it computes nothing.

Every constructor argument is accepted and validated the same way, so a configuration TensorWeaver refuses is refused here too::

>>> from tensorweaver import MockTensorWeaver
>>> MockTensorWeaver(usegpu=True, algorithm="vmpoa")
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: usegpu=True requires algorithm in ('dmpo', 'cmpo'), ...

and one it accepts is accepted::

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> sim = MockTensorWeaver(bonddim=64)
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
...
>>> c.push(mc.Measure(), 0, 0)
...
>>> res = sim.execute(c, nsamples=10)
>>> len(res.cstates)
10

Strict keeps memory at max_bond_dim and can cost accuracy, which the returned fidelity shows; "cmpo" with True raises BondDimensionError. See Strict and relaxed bond dimension mps.apply_mpo_dmpo(mpo, sv_cutoff=None, *, strict_bonddim=None) Wrapper for algorithm="dmpo" mps.apply_mpo_cmpo(mpo, sv_cutoff=None, *, strict_bonddim=None) Wrapper for algorithm="cmpo" mps.apply_mpo_vmpoa(mpo, sv_cutoff=None, *, strict_bonddim=None) Wrapper for algorithm="vmpoa" mps.apply_mpo_vmpob(mpo, sv_cutoff=None, *, strict_bonddim=None) Wrapper for algorithm="vmpob" mps.compress(sv_cutoff=None) Global compression sweep, restoring canonical form. None or non-positive uses the library default 1e-7

The default algorithm differs by level

apply_mpo defaults to "dmpo", the low-level primitive's own default. TwSimulator and execute() default to "vmpoa", which is more accurate at a given bond dimension. Driving the MPS yourself does not inherit the simulator's choice.

Deferred compression

Skipping the per-call compression sweep and running one pass at a quiet point is faster for a batch of two-qubit gates:

import numpy as np
import tensorweaver as tw

mps = tw.MPS.zero_state(64, max_bond_dim=256)
mpo = tw.MPO.identity(64, max_bond_dim=16)

mpo.apply_cx(0, 1)
mpo.apply_cz(2, 3)
mps.apply_mpo(mpo, post_compress=False)

gate = np.eye(4, dtype=np.complex128)      # any 4x4 unitary
mps.apply_gate_2q(gate, 4, 5)

# One sweep at quiescence: before measuring, reading an observable,
# or at the end of the circuit.
mps.compress()

Deferring the sweep leaves the state out of canonical form, so a later truncation compares singular values that are no longer the physical Schmidt weights. Batch only gates you know keep the bond dimension well below the cap, and prefer "cmpo" or "vmpoa" if unsure. See canonical form.

Noise channels (return (fidelity, index), where index is the 0-based sampled Kraus operator or unitary)

With validate=True (the default), Kraus channels check completeness (‖Σᵢ Kᵢ† Kᵢ − I‖_F ≤ 1e-8) and mixed-unitary channels check that the probabilities sum to 1 within 1e-8. Failures raise KrausCompletenessError. An incomplete operator set produces a non-physical state silently, which is why the check is on by default; validate=False is for post-selection and projective channels, where incompleteness is intended.

docs.title: RoutedMPS
docs.text:
The state behind TwDirectSimulator: an MPS whose qubits move along the chain as gates are routed, with the map from each qubit to its site. Every method takes 0-based logical qubits and every read-out answers in that numbering. No method builds an MPO.

import numpy as np
from tensorweaver import RoutedMPS

state = RoutedMPS.zero_state(6, 32)
h = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]], dtype=complex) / np.sqrt(2)
cx = np.eye(4, dtype=complex)[[0, 1, 3, 2]]
state.apply_gate(h, [0])
state.apply_gate(cx, [0, 5])    # qubit 5 is swapped next to qubit 0, and stays
print(state.layout)             # [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1]: qubit 5 sits on site 1
mps, fidelity = state.to_mps()  # sort back: qubit i on site i

docs.title: tensorweaver.visualization.plotbonds(state, mimiqstyle=True)
docs.text:
Plot the bond dimension and the entanglement entropy along the chain.

The top panel shows the bond dimension χ of every interior bond on a log-2 scale, with max_bond_dim as a dashed line. A bond that has reached that line is drawn red: it holds as many Schmidt values as the simulator allows, so any further weight on that cut was discarded. A state can also fit its cap exactly, a GHZ state at χ = 2 for one, so red marks where truncation can happen; the fidelity of the run and :func:plotschmidt tell how much it cost. Bonds below the line can still be truncated by sv_cutoff. The bottom panel shows the von Neumann entropy of each cut, in nats, which tells how much entanglement the bond carries.

Name Type Description Default state TwState | MPS

a :class:TwState, such as the first value returned by :meth:TwSimulator.evolvezerostate, or an :class:MPS.

required mimiqstyle bool

True

Name Type Description The Figure

Example::

import mimiqcircuits as mc
import tensorweaver as tw
from tensorweaver.visualization import plotbonds

# A 12-qubit brickwork of RY rotations and CX bricks.
c = mc.Circuit()
for layer in range(6):
    for q in range(12):
        c.push(mc.GateRY(0.5 + 0.1 * q), q)
    for q in range(layer % 2, 11, 2):
        c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)

# χ = 4 is too small for this depth: the middle bonds reach the cap.
state, _ = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=4, strict_bonddim=False).evolvezerostate(c)
fig = plotbonds(state)
fig.savefig("bonds.png")

docs.title: tensorweaver.visualization.BondWindow
docs.text:
A window that follows the bond structure of a :class:TwState as it evolves.

The window shows what :func:plotbonds shows. It is drawn when created and changes only when :meth:update is called: the state is read as it is then, and the picture moves there gradually. Bond dimensions grow on the log-2 axis, bars fade to red as they reach the cap, and the entropies follow. Between two updates the state can be evolved by any number of instructions.

The window needs an interactive matplotlib backend such as QtAgg or TkAgg, which in turn needs PyQt / PySide or Tk installed. In Jupyter, run %matplotlib qt first. With a non-interactive backend nothing opens and :meth:update redraws the figure in one step. In a script, the window only repaints during :meth:update; end with matplotlib.pyplot.show() to keep it open and responsive.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state TwState | MPS

the :class:TwState (or :class:MPS) to follow. Reading it moves the orthogonality center, which changes no amplitude.

required mimiqstyle bool

draw with the MIMIQ matplotlib style (default True).

True duration float

default length of an :meth:update animation, in seconds.

1.0

Example::

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mimiqcircuits as mc
import tensorweaver as tw
from tensorweaver.visualization import BondWindow

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=16, strict_bonddim=False)
state = sim.build_state(20)          # |0...0>: every bond at χ = 1
window = BondWindow(state)

layer = mc.Circuit()
for q in range(20):
    layer.push(mc.GateRY(0.7), q)
for q in range(19):
    layer.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)
step = sim.compile(layer)

for _ in range(6):
    sim.evolve(state, step)          # as many gates as you like...
    window.update()                  # ...then one animation to the new state

plt.show()                           # keep the window open at the end

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
This page explains the data model TensorWeaver works with, and the handful of numbers that decide whether a run is fast, accurate, or both. It assumes you are comfortable with quantum circuits (qubits, gates, measurement) but not with tensor networks.

Read it before choosing bonddim. It is the page that decides whether you pick sane parameters.

docs.title: Why not store the state vector?
docs.text:
A pure state of \(n\) qubits is a vector of \(2^n\) complex amplitudes:

\[ |\psi\rangle = \sum_{x \in \{0,1\}^n} c_x \, |x\rangle . \]

Storing every \(c_x\) is exact, and doubles in cost with each added qubit. Around 30 qubits this reaches tens of gigabytes, and beyond roughly 50 it is out of reach on any machine. A state-vector simulator pays that cost whatever the circuit does.

Most circuits of practical interest do not fill the full \(2^n\)-dimensional space. They produce states with limited entanglement, and those states can be written with far fewer numbers. A Matrix Product State stores only as much as the entanglement requires.

docs.title: From a state vector to an MPS
docs.text:
Take the amplitude tensor \(c_{s_1 s_2 \dots s_n}\), one index \(s_i \in \{0,1\}\) per qubit, and factor it into a chain of smaller tensors, one per qubit:

\[ c_{s_1 s_2 \dots s_n} = \sum_{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_{n-1}} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} \, A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1 \alpha_2} \, \cdots \, A^{s_n}_{\alpha_{n-1}} . \]

Each tensor \(A^{s_i}\) carries one physical index \(s_i\) (the qubit it represents) and one or two bond indices \(\alpha\) linking it to its neighbours. Drawn as a diagram it is a chain: a node per qubit, a horizontal bond between neighbours, and a physical leg hanging off each node.

The bond indices are where the entanglement lives. How many values \(\alpha_i\) runs over is the bond dimension at that link.

docs.title: Bond dimension
docs.text:
The bond dimension, written \(\chi\), is the quantity everything else follows from. Cut the chain between qubits \(i\) and \(i+1\). By the Schmidt decomposition the state across that cut is

\[ |\psi\rangle = \sum_{k=1}^{\chi_i} \lambda_k \, |L_k\rangle \otimes |R_k\rangle , \]

with Schmidt coefficients \(\lambda_k \ge 0\) in decreasing order. The number of non-zero terms is the Schmidt rank, and it is exactly the bond dimension needed at that cut.

State \(\chi\) required Product state, no entanglement 1 at every cut Bell pair, GHZ of any length 2 Volume-law entangled region \(2^{\min(i,\,n-i)}\), the worst case

An MPS with maximum bond dimension \(\chi\) stores about \(n \chi^2\) complex numbers instead of \(2^n\). In the worst case \(\chi\) reaches \(2^{n/2}\) and the MPS is as large as the state vector, buying nothing. Everything in between is where MPS simulation pays off.

\(\chi\) also sets the runtime: the cost of applying a two-qubit gate grows like \(\chi^3\). Doubling bonddim costs roughly eight times the work per gate and four times the memory.

docs.title: Truncation and what it costs
docs.text:
Most circuits would need a steadily growing \(\chi\) to stay exact. Two controls bound it:

Control Default Effect bonddim 256 Hard cap on \(\chi\). Never exceeded. sv_cutoff 1e-7 Discard Schmidt coefficients below this threshold.

After a gate or operator is applied, each affected bond is re-factored with a singular value decomposition and the smallest Schmidt coefficients are dropped until both controls are satisfied. sv_cutoff removes weight that is numerically negligible and usually costs nothing; bonddim is the control that bites, because it truncates whether or not the discarded weight is small.

Discarding weight is an approximation, and the state you keep is no longer the state the circuit defines.

Two further controls bound the operator rather than the state, and the tightest control in play is what limits a run. See Cutoffs and bond dimension for how the four compose and how to tell which one is binding.

docs.title: Reading the reported fidelity
docs.text:
Every run reports how much was discarded, as a fidelity: an estimate of the squared overlap between the truncated state and the untruncated one.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=1000, bonddim=64)
print(results.fidelities)      # one entry per evolution

results.fidelities holds one value per evolution: a single entry in sampling mode, and nsamples entries in trajectory mode. A value of 1.0 means nothing was discarded. A value of 0.98 means the kept state carries about 98% of the weight. results.avggateerrors reports the same information as an average error per two-qubit gate.

Two properties matter when you act on the number.

It is a lower bound, not a measurement. The value accumulates the weight discarded at each truncation. The true overlap with the exact state is at least this large, and often larger, because discarded pieces can fail to matter for the observable you care about.

A fidelity of 1.0 is necessary, not sufficient. The estimate covers truncation. It does not detect a state that has gone wrong for another reason, and it is reported per evolution rather than per observable. A run can report 1.0 and still carry a state whose overlap with the exact answer is well below that.

So use the fidelity as a screen, not as a certificate. To establish that a result is converged, vary the parameter that controls the approximation:

for chi in (16, 32, 64, 128, 256):
    r = execute(c, nsamples=1000, bonddim=chi, seed=1)
    print(chi, r.fidelities[0], r.histogram())

When the observable you care about stops moving as bonddim grows, the answer is converged. When it is still moving, the fidelity was not telling you the whole story. A mirror circuit (apply \(U\) then \(U^\dagger\) and check the return to \(|0\dots0\rangle\)) is the other standard check, and it tests the state rather than the bookkeeping.

Example 05 in the bundled examples runs this sweep and compares against a high-\(\chi\) reference.

docs.title: Canonical form and the orthogonality center
docs.text:
Truncation is only well defined when the singular values being compared are the physical Schmidt coefficients. That requires the chain to be in canonical form around an orthogonality center: every tensor left of the center is left-orthogonal, every tensor right of it is right-orthogonal. In that gauge an SVD at the center reads off the true Schmidt spectrum, so dropping the smallest values discards the smallest physical weight.

Operations move the center to where they act and restore the form afterwards, so ordinary use through execute() never needs to think about it. mps.orth_center reports the current position.

It becomes visible in two places:

  • Low-level editing. Writing site tensors directly with set_tensor() can break the form. Call recanonicalize() afterwards.
  • Deferred compression. post_compress=False and the direct apply_gate_2q path skip the sweep that restores canonical form, trading it for speed. The state then sits in a gauge where a later truncation is comparing the wrong numbers, which is why both are paired with an explicit mps.compress() at a quiet point. post_compress is on by default and should stay on unless you have measured that deferring it is safe for your circuits.

docs.title: Operators as tensor trains: the MPO
docs.text:
A Matrix Product Operator is the operator analogue of an MPS: a chain of tensors, each with an input and an output physical leg, representing a \(2^n \times 2^n\) operator in factored form.

TensorWeaver accumulates a run of unitary gates into an MPO and applies the whole operator to the state in one sweep, which costs less than applying the gates one at a time. entdim (default 16) caps the bond dimension of that operator. When the accumulated gates would exceed it, the operator is applied and a fresh one started, so entdim sets how many gates batch together rather than limiting which circuits can run. TwDirectSimulator builds no MPO and applies each gate to the state on its own; see Gate-by-gate simulation.

One case is an error rather than a flush: a single gate whose operator rank exceeds entdim cannot be compressed at all, and raises RuntimeError telling you to raise entdim. It is never silently approximated.

Applying an MPO to a state grows the bond dimension, which is then truncated back, so the choice of algorithm affects accuracy:

algorithm Name Character "vmpoa" (default) variational MPO application, variant a Variational sweeps, single-site. Most accurate at a given bonddim. "vmpob" variational MPO application, variant b Variational sweeps, two-site. "cmpo" canonical MPO application Single pass, truncating against the state's own Schmidt spectrum. Accuracy near the variational sweeps at close to single-pass cost. "dmpo" direct MPO application Single pass. The cheapest per application.

"vmpoa" is the default because accuracy at a fixed bonddim is usually worth more than throughput: if "dmpo" forces you to raise bonddim to recover the same fidelity, it is not the cheaper option.

"cmpo" is the one to try when neither trade appeals. It is a single pass, like "dmpo", arranged so that the weight it discards is chosen against the state's own Schmidt spectrum. Where the ceiling binds it keeps more of the state and tends to leave the state narrower, which makes the gates that follow cheaper too. The gain is largest on circuits whose true width sits below the ceiling; where the state genuinely exceeds it, no single pass does well and the variational sweeps keep the advantage.

While an operator is applied, its intermediates are wider than the result. strict_bonddim says whether they too are held to bonddim. By default "dmpo", "vmpoa" and "vmpob" are strict: memory follows from bonddim, at a possible cost in accuracy that the reported fidelity shows, and they need bonddim >= entdim; below it the simulator refuses to build. "dmpo" loses the most. Relaxed (strict_bonddim=False) uses more memory and is exact whenever the result fits. "cmpo" is relaxed and has no strict form; asking for one is an error.

Choosing an algorithm works through the decision, including strict and relaxed bond dimension.

docs.title: Why qubit order matters
docs.text:
An MPS is a one-dimensional chain, so entanglement between adjacent qubits is cheap and entanglement between distant qubits is expensive. A gate on qubits 0 and 40 forces a large bond dimension across everything between them. Relabelling qubits so interacting pairs sit close together can lower \(\chi\) for the same circuit by a large factor.

execute() does this when you ask for it, with reorderqubits=True; it is off by default, and it is chosen per run rather than per simulator. It reads the two-qubit gate graph, picks a permutation that keeps interacting qubits near each other, evolves in that order, and maps every result back to your original qubit labelling.

For when reordering pays, how to measure whether it does, and what it leaves alone, see Qubit ordering.

docs.title: Sampling mode and trajectory mode
docs.text:
execute() picks one of two modes from the circuit's content. The mode decides what nsamples means and how much work a run is.

Sampling mode Trajectory mode Chosen when The circuit is unitary, apart from trailing measurements The circuit contains a mid-circuit measurement, reset, IfStatement, or noise channel Evolutions One nsamples, each from a fresh state nsamples means Bitstrings drawn from the final state Independent runs of the whole circuit Cost One evolution plus cheap sampling Scales linearly with nsamples results.fidelities One entry nsamples entries

Sampling mode is far cheaper: the expensive part happens once and shots are drawn from the resulting state. Trailing measurements do not cost you this, because they are stripped before evolution and reapplied when samples are mapped onto classical bits.

Trajectory mode is required when the circuit branches. A measurement collapses the state, so every shot follows a different history and each one needs its own evolution. Noise channels are the same: each trajectory samples one branch of the channel, and the ensemble over trajectories reproduces the mixed state. Raising nsamples in trajectory mode raises the cost proportionally.

One consequence worth knowing before you rely on it: an amplitude requested in trajectory mode, whether through bitstrings= or an Amplitude instruction, reports the last trajectory's state rather than an ensemble average. Amplitudes are a pure-state quantity, and a trajectory ensemble is a mixed state.

Z-variable observations (Amplitude, BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy, ExpectationValue) read the state without collapsing it, so they never push a circuit into trajectory mode.

docs.title: Relationship to MIMIQ
docs.text:
TensorWeaver is a simulator for MIMIQ, not a separate circuit language. You build circuits with mimiqcircuits and the objects you already use carry over:

MIMIQ object Role in TensorWeaver Circuit, c.push(gate, *qubits) The circuit to simulate. Gates (GateH, GateCX, GateRX, ...) Decomposed to TensorWeaver's native set, then applied. Measure, Reset, IfStatement Select trajectory mode; handled inline per shot. BitString Measurement outcomes and amplitude queries. Z-variable ops (Amplitude, ExpectationValue, BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy) Non-destructive observations written to the z-register. QCSResults The return value of execute(): samples, amplitudes, fidelities, timings.

Where a concept is a MIMIQ concept rather than a TensorWeaver one, such as how gates are defined or what a BitString contains, the MIMIQ documentation is the reference.

Bitstring / qubit ordering

TensorWeaver uses little-endian by qubit index: bitstring position i is qubit i, so bs[0] is qubit 0. This is the opposite of Qiskit's convention, so bitstrings from results.cstates, results.histogram(), and mps.sample_bitstring() appear reversed relative to Qiskit output. The same convention applies to any BitString you pass to mps.amplitude() or execute(..., bitstrings=...).

docs.title: Gate-by-gate simulation
docs.text:
TwSimulator fuses runs of gates into a matrix product operator (MPO) and applies each one to the state in a single sweep. TwDirectSimulator builds no MPO at all: every gate updates the state on its own. It takes the same execute(circuit, nsamples=..., seed=...) call and returns the same QCSResults, so switching between the two is a one-line change.

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorweaver import TwDirectSimulator

c = mc.Circuit()
c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 9)          # qubits 0 and 9 are far apart on the chain
c.push(mc.Measure(), range(10), range(10))

results = TwDirectSimulator(bonddim=64).execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=1)

docs.title: How a gate is applied
docs.text:
• A one-qubit gate acts on the site of its qubit.
  • A two-qubit gate acts on two neighbouring sites: they are contracted together, the gate is applied, and one truncated SVD splits them back. Qubits that are not neighbours are first brought together by swapping adjacent sites.
  • A gate on three to max_gate_qubits (default 4) qubits gathers them into one block of sites and acts there in one step. A larger gate is decomposed.

Qubits move and stay moved. The swaps that route a gate are not undone. The state keeps a map from each qubit to the site that holds it, so a second gate on the same pair needs no routing. Every read-out (sampling, measurement, Amplitude, ExpectationValue) answers in your qubit numbering, wherever the qubits sit, so nothing is sorted during execute. evolvezerostate sorts the chain back at the end and returns a plain MPS with qubit i on site i.

Every swap is a truncated SVD at sv_cutoff and bonddim, like a gate, and what it discards is included in the reported fidelity.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
routing= decides which of a gate's two qubits moves.

  • "lookahead" (default) considers both. A move qualifies if every bond its swaps cross is at most half of bonddim: a swap there cannot truncate, since it at most doubles a bond. Among the qualifying moves it takes the one that leaves the next 16 two-qubit gates closest. When neither qualifies, it moves the gate's second qubit, as "target" does.
  • "target" always moves the gate's second qubit next to its first. For a CX that brings the target to the control, which keeps a control that acts on many targets in place.

Near the cap, keeping the first qubit fixed holds entangled qubits together; minimising swaps there instead costs fidelity. Where the state is weakly entangled, every swap is exact and the lookahead only saves work. On the 100-qubit MQT Bench u3+cx circuits the lookahead was 1.1 to 3.6x faster than "target" on 11 of 13 inputs, up to 1.4x slower on the other two.

docs.title: Which simulator to use
docs.text:
TwSimulator TwDirectSimulator Cost per gate one sweep per fused block of gates one SVD per two-qubit gate, plus the routing swaps Strongest on deep, dense layers of two-qubit gates, ladders of CX that fuse into a small operator controlled long-range gates (QFT, phase estimation, amplitude estimation), circuits whose state stays weakly entangled BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy yes no: they read a bond of the chain, which is in whatever order routing left it Noise channels one or two qubits one or two qubits GPU usegpu=True no

Measured on 100-qubit MQT Bench circuits (one thread, the circuit plus 1000 samples): TwDirectSimulator was 1.8 to 8.5x faster than TwSimulator on qft, qftentangled, amplitude and phase estimation and on the 125-qubit quantum walk. It could not run su2random and realamprandom at all: their ladders of CX gates fuse into a low-rank operator, while applied one at a time every intermediate state is fully entangled. TwSimulator runs both at bond dimension 16.

When in doubt, run the circuit on both at a small bonddim and compare the time and the reported fidelity.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning bonddim 256 maximum bond dimension sv_cutoff None (1e-7) singular values below this are discarded by every gate and swap max_gate_qubits 4 the most qubits a gate may act on before it is decomposed; a gate on k qubits contracts k sites into one tensor of 4**k · χ² entries routing "lookahead" which qubit a two-qubit gate moves, see above seed, linalg as for TwSimulator

entdim, mpo_cutoff, algorithm, strict_bonddim, post_compress, buffer and traversal are MPO settings and have no counterpart here. reorderqubits= on execute works as for TwSimulator: a good starting layout means fewer swaps.

docs.title: The routed state
docs.text:
RoutedMPS is the state behind the simulator, usable on its own:

import numpy as np
from tensorweaver import RoutedMPS

state = RoutedMPS.zero_state(6, 32)
h = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]], dtype=complex) / np.sqrt(2)
cx = np.eye(4, dtype=complex)[[0, 1, 3, 2]]
state.apply_gate(h, [0])
state.apply_gate(cx, [0, 5])    # qubit 5 is swapped next to qubit 0, and stays
print(state.layout)             # [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1]: qubit 5 sits on site 1
mps, fidelity = state.to_mps()  # sort back: qubit i on site i

The engine always moves a gate's second qubit; the "lookahead" routing is applied by this package, which picks the mover by the order it passes the qubits in. See the API reference for every method, and example 14_direct_simulator for a walk-through.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Sixteen runnable scripts ship with the package, ordered so each builds on the ones before it. They cover the simulator from a first Bell pair through noise, qubit layout, the low-level MPS/MPO API, engine selection, qudits, the Qiskit integration, and gate-by-gate simulation. Each is deterministic for a fixed seed. The two 00_ scripts run without a licence, on the public wheel; the rest need the licensed one.

docs.title: Where they are
docs.text:
The examples are bundled inside the installed package:

import tensorweaver as tw
print(tw.examples_dir())   # .../site-packages/tensorweaver/examples

From a source checkout they live in tensorweaver-python/python/tensorweaver/examples/.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
import subprocess, sys, tensorweaver as tw

script = tw.examples_dir() / "01_bell_pair" / "main.py"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(script)])

Or directly from a source checkout. Build both engines first, since the default engine is OpenBLAS and maturin develop alone does not compile it:

cd tensorweaver-python
scripts/dev-build.sh
uv run python python/tensorweaver/examples/01_bell_pair/main.py

Most scripts take flags such as --seed, --n, --shots, and --depth. Run one with --help for its options.

Needs the qiskit extra. 13 13_qudits d-level sites on the low-level API: zero_state_qudits / product_state_qudits, d×d gates and expectation values, a qutrit Kraus channel, and fusing two qubits into one d = 4 site. 14 14_direct_simulator TwDirectSimulator: gates applied one at a time with swap routing and no MPO, compared with MPO fusion on a QFT-like circuit; the two routings; the routed state and sorting it back.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
The examples are written to be read in order. If you already know what an MPS is, useful entry points are:

  • 05 for the χ-versus-fidelity trade-off.
  • 06 for noise and trajectory mode.
  • 07 for qubit layout.
  • 08 to 10 for the low-level surface that execute() uses internally.
  • 13 for qudits.

docs.title: Circuit Execution
docs.text:
execute() runs a mimiqcircuits circuit on the MPS engine and returns a QCSResults.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=1000, bonddim=64)
print(results.histogram())
print(results.fidelities[0])
print(results.timings)

execute() builds a fresh simulator per call. To reuse one configuration across many circuits, construct a TwSimulator instead and call its execute() method. The configuration keywords below map onto the constructor; nsamples, seed, and num_qubits stay per call.

docs.title: Parameter sweeps
docs.text:
A circuit with free symbols runs once per point of a parameter table. Build a SweepExperiment from the circuit and a ParameterTable, and pass it where a circuit goes. The result is a list of QCSResults, one per point, each run with its own seed derived from the run's seed.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateRX, Measure, SweepExperiment, gridtable
from symengine import symbols
from tensorweaver import TwSimulator

theta = symbols("theta")
c = Circuit()
c.push(GateRX(theta), 0)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)

# One point per angle; `gridtable` takes the Cartesian product when given
# several symbols.
ex = SweepExperiment(c, gridtable({theta: [0.0, 1.0, 3.14159]}))
results = TwSimulator(bonddim=32).execute(ex, nsamples=1000, seed=7)
print([r.histogram() for r in results])

The table must bind every free symbol of the circuit, and nothing else; the SweepExperiment constructor checks it. TwSimulator.execute(c, param_grid=[...]) with a list of dictionaries runs the same loop without the check.

docs.title: Execution modes
docs.text:
The mode is chosen from the circuit's content, and it decides what nsamples means. Concepts covers why.

Sampling mode Trajectory mode Chosen when Circuit is unitary apart from measurements that nothing depends on afterwards Circuit contains a measurement whose qubit is reused, a Reset, an IfStatement, or a noise channel Evolutions One nsamples nsamples means Bitstrings drawn from the final state Independent runs of the full circuit results.fidelities One entry nsamples entries

A measurement does not by itself force trajectory mode. Measurements that nothing later depends on are stripped before evolution and reapplied when samples are mapped onto classical bits, so the run stays in the cheap mode.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX, Measure
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)
c.push(Measure(), 1, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=1000, bonddim=64)
print(len(results.fidelities))   # 1: sampling mode, evolved once
print(results.histogram())       # e.g. {bs"00": 498, bs"11": 502}

Reusing a measured qubit makes each shot follow its own history, so each shot needs its own evolution:

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)   # qubit 0 is used again below
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=100, bonddim=64)
print(len(results.fidelities))   # 100: one per trajectory

Trajectory mode needs explicit measurements

In sampling mode every qubit is projected when the final state is sampled, so results.histogram() is populated even with no Measure in the circuit. In trajectory mode cstates come from the classical register, so a circuit with no Measure yields no classical states and an empty histogram. Push the measurements you want to read.

Amplitudes in trajectory mode

bitstrings=, and an in-circuit Amplitude(...), report the last trajectory's state, not an ensemble average. An amplitude is a pure-state quantity and a trajectory ensemble is a mixed state. To get ensemble statistics, aggregate over runs yourself.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: circuit and nsamples are positional; everything else is keyword-only.

docs.title: Accuracy and cost
docs.text: Parameter Default When to change it bonddim 256 The main accuracy/cost dial. Raise until your observable stops moving; lower for speed on lightly entangled circuits. Cost per two-qubit gate grows like bonddim³. sv_cutoff -1.0 (means 1e-7) Rarely. Lower it towards 1e-10 when you need tighter accuracy at a bonddim you are not saturating; raising it trades accuracy for speed. Any negative value selects the library default. algorithm "vmpoa" How each fused operator is applied. See Choosing an algorithm. strict_bonddim None Whether bonds may exceed bonddim while an operator is applied. None is strict for "dmpo", "vmpoa", "vmpob" and relaxed for "cmpo". Strict keeps memory bounded by bonddim and can cost accuracy, most for "dmpo"; the reported fidelity shows the loss. Strict needs bonddim >= entdim and raises ValueError otherwise. False is exact whenever the result fits, at more memory and time. "cmpo" with True raises ValueError. See Strict and relaxed bond dimension. entdim 16 Caps the bond dimension of the operator that gates accumulate into. Raise for deep, highly entangling segments so more gates batch per application. A single gate whose operator rank exceeds entdim raises RuntimeError. post_compress True Leave on. Off defers the sweep that restores canonical form, which is faster on circuits well below bonddim but lets later truncations compare the wrong singular values. Turn it off only after measuring that your circuits are unaffected. max_bond_dim None Deprecated alias for bonddim. Overrides bonddim when set. Use bonddim.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Parameter Default When to change it reorderqubits None Off by default: the circuit evolves in the layout you wrote. True runs the whole portfolio of layout searches and keeps whichever result scores best against bonddim, or your own layout when none of them clearly beats it. Worth trying when the interaction graph has locality the numbering hides and the bond dimension is the limit. Naming one search ("greedy", "sa" / "simulated_annealing", "multilevel") pins it, which is mostly useful for comparing them. Leave it off when you need the MPS chain to keep your qubit numbering. num_qubits None Set it when the circuit does not touch every qubit of the register you want simulated. Inferred from the circuit otherwise.

Reordering, when you turn it on, is transparent: samples, amplitudes, and z-variables come back in your original qubit labelling. To tune the search's margin or alpha, pass a TwReorderQubitsPass to TwSimulator.execute through passes=; see Qubit ordering.

docs.title: Sampling and observation
docs.text: Parameter Default When to change it nsamples 1000 Shots in sampling mode, full evolutions in trajectory mode. Cost is flat in sampling mode and linear in trajectory mode. seed 42 Set it for reproducibility. Separate streams for sampling, noise, trajectories and randomised passes are derived from it, so trajectories differ from one another while the whole run repeats exactly. bitstrings None Pass a list of BitString to read specific amplitudes out of results.amplitudes.

docs.title: Circuit preparation
docs.text: Parameter Default When to change it traversal "sequential" Order gates are walked while they batch into operators. See Circuit traversal order. fuse None Fuses runs of gates into GateCustom blocks before evolution. None does not fuse. Distinct from, and usually redundant with, the operator batching applied during evolution. fuse_threshold None Minimum qubit count for fuse to act. Setting it alone also turns fusion on; with fuse=False it raises ValueError. canonicaldecompose None Decompose to the canonical basis before evolution. None does not decompose. simplify None Simplify the circuit before evolution: cancel inverse pairs, merge rotations, resynthesize one-qubit blocks. Two-qubit resynthesis is left out: it reorders the gates and slows the evolution. The unitary is kept exactly. None does not simplify. It runs before fuse and reorderqubits, so both see the shorter circuit. Worth trying on transpiled circuits, which often carry gates that cancel. buffer 0 Prepares up to buffer operators on a background thread while evolution applies the current one. Results are identical to 0. A depth of 2 to 4 is enough, since only one or two operators are in flight.

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
Parameter Default When to change it linalg None Selects the linear-algebra library: "openblas", "mkl" or "faer". See Linear-algebra engine. usemkl None Deprecated. True is linalg="mkl", False is linalg="openblas". usegpu False Runs the state on an NVIDIA GPU. Requires algorithm="dmpo" or "cmpo". See GPU engine.

Bitstring / qubit ordering

TensorWeaver uses little-endian by qubit index: bitstring position i is qubit i. This is the opposite of Qiskit's convention, so bitstrings from results.cstates and results.histogram(), and those passed via bitstrings=, appear reversed compared to equivalent Qiskit output.

docs.title: Return value: QCSResults
docs.text:
Field Type Contents cstates list[BitString] Classical states, one per sample or trajectory. In trajectory mode these come from the circuit's Measure instructions. fidelities list[float] Truncation fidelity per evolution. One entry in sampling mode, nsamples in trajectory mode. A lower bound: see reading the fidelity. avggateerrors list[float] The same information expressed as an average error per two-qubit gate. amplitudes dict[BitString, complex] Amplitudes for each bitstring passed to bitstrings=. zstates list[list[complex]] Z-register values per evolution, written by z-variable operations. timings dict[str, float] Wall-clock seconds: "total", "compile" (decomposition and layout), "apply" (evolution), "sample". simulator str "TensorWeaver". version str Version of the installed mimiq-tensorweaver package.

Two methods are worth knowing:

  • results.histogram() returns dict[BitString, int], counting each classical state.
  • results.histzvars() returns dict[tuple, int], counting each z-state.

docs.title: Computing amplitudes
docs.text:
from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX, BitString
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

bs00, bs11 = BitString([0, 0]), BitString([1, 1])
results = execute(c, nsamples=1, bonddim=64, bitstrings=[bs00, bs11])

print(results.amplitudes[bs00])   # ~0.7071+0j
print(results.amplitudes[bs11])   # ~0.7071+0j

docs.title: Circuit traversal order (traversal)
docs.text:
A circuit is more than a flat list. Two instructions are ordered relative to each other only when they share a wire (a qubit, a classical bit, or a z-variable). traversal chooses how that freedom is used while gates batch into operators.

Value Order "sequential" (default) The circuit's insertion order. "bfs" Breadth-first topological order: independent gates group into layers. "dfs" Depth-first topological order: one dependency chain is followed to its end before backtracking.

Reordering is confined to the gates between instructions that read or change the state. Measurement, reset, noise channels, observables (Amplitude, BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy, ExpectationValue), barriers, and conditionals stay where they are and act as synchronisation points.

All three produce the same simulated state. They differ in how gates batch, which changes the intermediate bond dimension and therefore runtime and memory. "bfs" tends to pack each operator with more mutually commuting gates, which helps on circuits with wide, shallow layers. "sequential" matches a literal reading of the circuit.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorweaver import TwSimulator

circuit = Circuit()
for q in range(8):
    circuit.push(GateH(), q)
for q in range(0, 8, 2):
    circuit.push(GateCX(), q, q + 1)

sim = TwSimulator(bonddim=128, traversal="bfs")
results = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, seed=42)

docs.title: Linear-algebra engine (linalg)
docs.text:
The dense linear algebra underneath the MPS runs on one of three libraries. Each is compiled into a separate native module, selected per simulator:

linalg Engine Availability None (default) Whichever this build ships, OpenBLAS for preference Always works: the default is resolved from the engines actually installed. "openblas" OpenBLAS Linux and macOS. Vendored into the wheel; works from a plain pip install with no system BLAS. "mkl" Intel MKL Linux x86_64 and Windows. Comes from the mkl package, a dependency of those wheels. "faer" faer Every platform. Pure Rust, links no system library. Usually slower than the other two, so it is never the default when another engine is installed. 
from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorweaver import TwSimulator, execute

circuit = Circuit()
circuit.push(GateH(), 0)
circuit.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

sim = TwSimulator(linalg="mkl")                           # whole simulator
results = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000)

results = execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, linalg="mkl")   # one call

Which engines a wheel contains depends on the platform: Linux ships all three, macOS arm64 ships OpenBLAS and faer (MKL is x86-only), and Windows ships MKL and faer. This is why the default is None rather than an engine name: a fixed OpenBLAS default would ask the Windows wheel for a module it does not have. The resolved choice is readable afterwards as sim.linalg.

An explicit linalg is never quietly switched. linalg="openblas" on Windows asks for an engine that is not installed and raises ImportError saying so, rather than running on MKL behind your back. Leave the keyword out to get whatever this platform provides. An unknown name raises ValueError.

docs.title: usemkl (deprecated)
docs.text: usemkl is the older spelling and still works, with a DeprecationWarning: usemkl=True is linalg="mkl" and usemkl=False is linalg="openblas". Passing both with different engines raises ValueError. sim.usemkl still reads back whether the simulator runs on MKL, also with a warning.

docs.title: Why MKL is a dependency and not part of the wheel
docs.text:
OpenBLAS is an ordinary shared library, so it is bundled into the wheel. MKL is not: libmkl_rt is a dispatcher that loads its backing libraries (libmkl_core, libmkl_intel_thread, the ISA kernels) by name at call time, so they never appear in the wheel's import table and no wheel-repair tool can find them. Bundling the dispatcher alone would be worse than bundling nothing, since the engine would import and then die on the first BLAS call.

So the wheels that carry an MKL engine, Linux x86_64 and Windows, carry no MKL library at all and depend on the PyPI mkl package instead. pip install mimiq-tensorweaver brings it in, and tensorweaver opens it before importing the engine, so nothing has to be set in the environment. That package installs into a directory no library search path knows about, which is why opening it explicitly is necessary: LD_LIBRARY_PATH is read once when the process starts and cannot be set from inside it.

Any other complete MKL works too, as long as its libmkl_rt major version matches the one the wheel was built against: a conda mkl, a distribution package, or Intel oneAPI's setvars.sh.

Requesting linalg="mkl" without a usable runtime raises an ImportError explaining how to install it, or, on a platform with no MKL build at all, saying so instead. The check runs up front in a short subprocess, so you get a Python exception rather than MKL aborting the process mid-operation.

docs.title: GPU engine (usegpu)
docs.text:
usegpu=True runs the state on an NVIDIA GPU. Linux x86_64 only.

pip install "mimiq-tensorweaver[cuda]"

The engine is in the published Linux x86_64 wheels; the extra adds the CUDA maths libraries it loads. The macOS and Windows wheels have no GPU engine.

Driver requirement

The wheels are built with CUDA 12.9, and the device kernel ships as PTX that the driver compiles on the fly. So the driver has to be at least as new as that release: 575.51.03 or newer. An older driver loads the engine and fails when the kernel is first used. nvidia-smi reports the version it is running.

The CUDA libraries themselves come from the extra, not from the system, so no CUDA toolkit installation is needed on the machine that runs this.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorweaver import TwSimulator

circuit = Circuit()
circuit.push(GateH(), 0)
circuit.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

sim = TwSimulator(usegpu=True, algorithm="cmpo", bonddim=512)
results = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000)

The state is moved into device memory once, evolved there, and moved back once, so a circuit pays one transfer at each end rather than one per gate. A transfer over PCIe costs more than the truncated SVD it would feed, which is why the residency is what makes the GPU worth using at all.

docs.title: It is not always faster
docs.text:
The device wins where the state is large and loses where it is small: each site's truncated SVD carries a fixed launch cost the host does not pay. On an NVIDIA A30 against one Xeon core, a 24-qubit brick-layer circuit of depth 24:

bonddim CPU (s) GPU (s) Speed-up 64 0.35 0.44 0.8x 128 1.41 0.51 2.8x 256 6.35 0.78 8.2x 512 27.8 1.16 24x

So below roughly bonddim=64 the GPU is slower, and the case for it grows with the problem: over those four circuits the CPU's time grows 80x while the GPU's grows under 3x. Both engines truncate identically and the reported fidelities agree to every digit printed, so the speed-up is not bought with accuracy.

The CPU column is one core
