Single-threaded OpenBLAS, which is that machine's fastest configuration for this workload rather than a handicapped one, and MKL is not in the comparison at all. Treat these as orders of magnitude, not as a benchmark.

docs.title: What it requires, and what it refuses
docs.text:
• algorithm="dmpo" or algorithm="cmpo" is required. Only the two single-pass algorithms have a device implementation; the variational sweeps ("vmpoa", the default, and "vmpob") run on the host. The simulator raises rather than switching for you: the algorithms do not return the same state once truncation binds, so changing it silently would make the same arguments answer differently depending on the hardware. Prefer "cmpo", the accurate one of the two.
  • linalg must be unset or "openblas". The CUDA engine is a single module whose host provider is OpenBLAS, so linalg="mkl" or "faer" with usegpu=True raises ValueError.
  • Circuits needing trajectory mode are refused: a mid-circuit Measure or Reset, a noise channel, or qubit loss. None of these has a device path, so running one would transfer the whole state back and forth per operation, which is slower than staying on the host. Use usegpu=False for those.

Sampling and amplitudes are host operations, and the state is brought back for them automatically, so nothing extra is needed to read results.

docs.title: When there is no GPU
docs.text:
The engine module links no CUDA library: the driver and the maths libraries are loaded by name at call time. So it imports on any machine, and asking for the device is what fails, with an ImportError naming the fix. To check first:

from tensorweaver._engine import get_core

try:
    get_core(usegpu=True)    # loads the CUDA engine and probes for a device
    has_gpu = True
except ImportError as err:   # no CUDA engine in this build, or no usable GPU
    has_gpu = False
    print(err)

The [cuda] extra supplies cuBLAS and cuSOLVER. The NVIDIA driver itself is not redistributable and must come from the system; nvidia-smi working is the usual sign that it is there.

Those two libraries do not have to be on any library search path. The extra installs them under site-packages/nvidia/, which the loader knows nothing about, so selecting the CUDA engine opens them from there by absolute path first. Setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH is neither needed nor harmful, and a CUDA runtime already installed system-wide is used exactly as before.

docs.title: Engines do not share objects
docs.text:
Objects are engine-specific

The engines are independent native modules. They can run side by side in one process, but their objects do not interoperate: an MPS, MPO, Rng, or TwState from one engine cannot be passed to a simulator or method backed by the other, and attempting it raises TypeError. Move a state across by serialising it:

from tensorweaver import TwSimulator

sim_ob  = TwSimulator(linalg="openblas")
sim_mkl = TwSimulator(linalg="mkl")

state = sim_ob.build_state(3)
blob = state.mps.serialize()                      # protobuf bytes, a copy
mps_mkl = sim_mkl._core.PyMps.deserialize(blob)   # usable by the MKL engine

Both engines compute the same results, so a workflow normally stays on one engine end to end.

docs.title: TensorWeaverBasis
docs.text: TensorWeaverBasis defines which operations run natively, without decomposition.

docs.title: Terminal operations
docs.text: Operation Handling GateRX(θ), GateRY(θ), GateRZ(λ) Applied directly. GateU(θ, φ, λ, γ) Applied directly. GateID Skipped. GateCX, GateCZ, GateISWAP Applied directly. Any two-qubit unitary Applied from its matrix. Control(n, 1Q-gate) Applied as a multi-controlled gate, for any number of controls. Measure Collapses the state, stores the outcome in the classical register. Reset, MeasureReset Measure, then a conditional X back to |0⟩. IfStatement(op, bs) Applies op when the classical bits match bs. Terminal when op is. Amplitude, BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy, ExpectationValue Read the state into the z-register. Any krauschannel Mixed-unitary or general Kraus channel, on one or two qubits. Classical logic (Not, And, Or, Xor, SetBit, ...) Applied to the classical register. Z-register arithmetic (Add, Multiply, Pow) Combines z-variables. Barrier A fusion boundary for the qubits it names; no effect on the state. Annotations (Detector, loss markers, ...) No simulation semantics.

docs.title: Decomposed operations
docs.text:
Everything else goes through the canonical rewrite, calling each gate's _decompose(). For example GateH becomes GateU(π/2, 0, π) and GateSWAP becomes three GateCX.

Multi-controlled gates

Control(n, 1Q-gate) is terminal for any number of controls: the operator is built directly rather than decomposed into a CX ladder. Toffoli (CCX), C3X, and higher-order controlled gates all take this path.

docs.title: Z-variable operations
docs.text:
Z-variable operations observe the state without changing it, writing into the circuit's z-register. They never push a circuit into trajectory mode.

Operation Arguments Stores Amplitude(bs) A BitString Complex amplitude ⟨bs\|ψ⟩ BondDim() A bond index Bond dimension, in the .real part SchmidtRank() A bond index Schmidt rank above a 1e-12 cutoff, in the .real part VonNeumannEntropy() A bond index Entanglement entropy in bits, in the .real part ExpectationValue(op) 1 or 2 qubits for a gate or matrix operator, any number for a PauliString Complex ⟨ψ\|op\|ψ⟩

BondDim, SchmidtRank, and VonNeumannEntropy take a bond index, naming the bipartition {0..k-1} | {k..n-1}, not a qubit. Qubit reordering keeps those cuts intact and leaves the index alone.

from mimiqcircuits import (
    Circuit, GateH, GateCX, GateZ,
    Amplitude, BondDim, SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy,
    ExpectationValue, BitString,
)
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

c.push(Amplitude(BitString([0, 0])), 0)      # -> z0
c.push(BondDim(), 1, 1)                      # bond 1 -> z1
c.push(SchmidtRank(), 1, 2)                  # bond 1 -> z2
c.push(VonNeumannEntropy(), 1, 3)            # bond 1 -> z3
c.push(ExpectationValue(GateZ()), 0, 4)      # -> z4

results = execute(c, nsamples=1, num_qubits=2, bonddim=64)
zs = results.zstates[0]
print(f"amplitude |00>     {zs[0]}")
print(f"bond dim at cut 1  {zs[1].real:.0f}")
print(f"Schmidt rank       {zs[2].real:.0f}")
print(f"entropy (bits)     {zs[3].real:.4f}")
print(f"<Z> on qubit 0     {zs[4].real:.4f}")

docs.title: Noise channels
docs.text:
Any krauschannel from mimiqcircuits on one or two qubits is applied directly. Mixed-unitary channels such as PauliX, Depolarizing, and PauliNoise are detected through ismixedunitary() and sample one unitary per shot. General channels such as AmplitudeDamping use the full operator-sum form.

Noise selects trajectory mode, so nsamples becomes the number of independent evolutions, and the ensemble over them reproduces the mixed state. Push the measurements you want to read: in trajectory mode the histogram comes from the classical register.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX, PauliX, Measure
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(PauliX(0.05), 0)     # 5% bit-flip on qubit 0
c.push(PauliX(0.05), 1)     # 5% bit-flip on qubit 1
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)
c.push(Measure(), 1, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=500, bonddim=64)
print(results.histogram())   # weight leaks onto 01 and 10

docs.title: Conditional operations
docs.text:
IfStatement(op, bitstring) applies op only when the classical register matches. It selects trajectory mode.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateX, Measure, IfStatement, BitString
from tensorweaver import execute

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)
c.push(IfStatement(GateX(), BitString("1")), 1, 0)   # X on qubit 1 if bit 0 is set
c.push(Measure(), 1, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=200, num_qubits=2, bonddim=64)
print(results.histogram())   # only 00 and 11 appear

docs.title: Using the basis directly
docs.text:
TensorWeaverBasis plugs into the mimiqcircuits decomposition API, which is useful for inspecting what a circuit lowers to before running it.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH
from mimiqcircuits.decomposition import decompose, eachdecomposed
from tensorweaver.basis import TensorWeaverBasis

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)

decomposed = decompose(c, TensorWeaverBasis())

for inst in eachdecomposed(c, TensorWeaverBasis()):   # streaming variant
    print(inst)

docs.title: Free-threaded Python
docs.text:
CPython 3.13 introduced a build with no global interpreter lock, and 3.14 is the first release where it is a supported configuration rather than an experiment. On such an interpreter Python threads run at the same time on different cores, so a single process can run several simulations in parallel without the cost of starting one process per run.

TensorWeaver supports it. This page covers how to install the right wheel, the one thing you must currently do to keep the GIL off, the rule your code has to follow, and how much threading actually buys.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Free-threaded interpreters are named with a t suffix: python3.14t. They are a separate installation from python3.14, and packages are not shared between them.

python3.14t -m pip install mimiq-tensorweaver

There is nothing extra to select. TensorWeaver publishes a dedicated free-threaded wheel and the installer picks it by tag:

Interpreter Wheel python3.11 … python3.14 cp311-abi3, one wheel for every version python3.14t cp314-cp314t, Linux x86_64: glibc 2.35 or newer, and glibc 2.34 for RHEL 9 and its rebuilds

The free-threaded wheel exists separately because a free-threaded interpreter has no stable ABI to build against, so it covers exactly one Python version rather than all of them. It carries the same engines as the ordinary Linux wheel: OpenBLAS, MKL, faer and CUDA.

The two wheels cannot be mixed up. A free-threaded interpreter does not accept abi3 wheels, so asking for one on python3.14t reports no matching distribution rather than installing something that would crash.

Two limitations for now. The free-threaded wheels are built for Linux x86_64 only; ask us if you need macOS or Windows. And the qiskit extra cannot be installed, because Qiskit publishes no free-threaded wheels yet.

docs.title: Keeping the GIL off: PYTHON_GIL=0
docs.text:
A free-threaded interpreter turns the GIL back on, for the whole process, as soon as it imports an extension module that has not declared itself free-thread-safe. It says so when it happens:

RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load
module 'symengine.lib.symengine_wrapper', which has not declared that it can
run safely without the GIL.

TensorWeaver's engines declare it, so importing tensorweaver never causes this. symengine does not, and mimiqcircuits imports symengine to build its gate matrices, so import mimiqcircuits re-enables the GIL. Once enabled it cannot be turned off again: the process keeps it for its lifetime.

Until symengine declares support, override the decision at startup:

PYTHON_GIL=0 python3.14t my_simulation.py
# or
python3.14t -X gil=0 my_simulation.py

Check that it worked before trusting a measurement:

import sys
import mimiqcircuits as mc
import tensorweaver as tw

print(sys._is_gil_enabled())   # must be False

PYTHON_GIL=0 overrides every module's declaration in the process, not just symengine's, which is why it is opt-in and why we do not enable it for you.

Two things make it a reasonable thing to ask for here. symengine's free-threading declaration is merged upstream and only waiting on a release, and its published wheels are already built thread-safe, so the override contradicts a stale declaration rather than running unprotected code (recorded in mimiqcircuits 0.27.1's changelog). And we have tested the path you are using: circuits executed across threads with the GIL forced off return results identical to a sequential run, including several threads executing the same Circuit object.

Even so, keep symbolic work out of your threads. Build and parametrise circuits before starting them, which is the normal shape anyway, and the override then covers a library your threads only read from.

docs.title: One object per thread
docs.text:
An MPS, MPO or Rng must be used by one thread at a time. The objects hold no shared state, so threads that each own theirs never interact. Two threads driving the same object is refused rather than silently corrupting it:

RuntimeError: Already borrowed

That is a Rust borrow conflict surfacing in Python, not a data race, but it is an error your code has to avoid rather than handle. Give each thread its own state:

import threading
import tensorweaver as tw

def run(seed, results, index):
    sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=256)          # one simulator per thread
    results[index] = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, seed=seed)

results = [None] * 8
threads = [
    threading.Thread(target=run, args=(seed, results, i))
    for i, seed in enumerate(range(8))
]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

Sharing the Circuit between threads, as above, is fine: execute reads it and builds its own state.

The same rule covers a GPU run: a state moved to the device with MPS.to_device() belongs to the thread that drives it. Threads that each hold their own device state work, but they share one device, so the parallelism you get is the device's, not the host's.

docs.title: What threading buys
docs.text:
The answer depends on which API you drive, because the heavy kernels already release the GIL on every build. MPO application, compression, recanonicalisation, sampling, expectation values and the noise channels all release it around the linear algebra, so several threads overlap their work on an ordinary python3.14 too. Per-gate calls such as apply_gate_2q do not: the kernel is a single small SVD measured in microseconds, and releasing the GIL around it would cost more than it saves.

So, for eight concurrent runs on an otherwise idle machine with enough cores:

What your threads call python3.14 python3.14t TwSimulator.execute, MPS.apply_mpo, sampling already scales, roughly 2 to 3× slightly better MPS.apply_gate_1q / apply_gate_2q in a loop no gain, threads take turns scales, roughly 3 to 4×

Measured on a random 18-qubit, depth-16 circuit at bond dimension 64, eight threads on 16 cores. Your numbers will differ; the shape is the point. If you are running circuits rather than driving the tensors directly, threading is already working for you and the free-threaded build is a refinement rather than the thing that unlocks it.

docs.title: Threads and BLAS threads multiply
docs.text:
Each simulation thread calls into BLAS, which is itself multi-threaded, so the process can end up asking for far more threads than the machine has cores. Oversubscription of that kind costs much more than the parallelism gains.

Size the two together: with n Python threads on c available cores, set

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$((c / n))

and never leave BLAS free to use every core in each of n threads. On a cluster, c is the cores your allocation actually holds, not the cores the node has. See Tuning a run for the rest of the performance controls.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Install the package, run a circuit, read the results. If Matrix Product State, bond dimension, or truncation are new to you, read Concepts first: this page assumes them.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Wheels are published on tagged releases to the QPerfect GitLab package registry, which requires authentication:

pip install mimiq-tensorweaver \
  --index-url https://__token__:<your-access-token>@gitlab.qperfect.io/api/v4/projects/29/packages/pypi/simple

To avoid repeating the index URL, configure it in ~/.pip/pip.conf:

[global]
index-url = https://__token__:<your-access-token>@gitlab.qperfect.io/api/v4/projects/29/packages/pypi/simple

then pip install mimiq-tensorweaver.

index-url, not extra-index-url. The same distribution name is published on public PyPI as the unlicensed mock (see Without a licence), and with both indexes in play pip is free to take either copy of a name it finds in both, so pip install -U could replace a licensed install with the mock. An exclusive index-url removes the ambiguity.

The registry does not proxy PyPI, so dependencies have to come from somewhere: pass --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple on the install, or keep a second [install] section for it, rather than demoting the QPerfect index back to an extra.

docs.title: With uv
docs.text:
uv does not read pip.conf. For a one-off install, pass the registry as an index:

uv pip install mimiq-tensorweaver \
  --index https://__token__:<your-access-token>@gitlab.qperfect.io/api/v4/projects/29/packages/pypi/simple

uv takes each package from the first index that has it, so the licensed wheel wins over the PyPI mock and every other dependency still comes from PyPI.

In a uv project, declare the registry in pyproject.toml and pin mimiq-tensorweaver to it:

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "qperfect"
url = "https://gitlab.qperfect.io/api/v4/projects/29/packages/pypi/simple"
explicit = true  # only packages pinned below are fetched from it

[tool.uv.sources]
mimiq-tensorweaver = { index = "qperfect" }

and keep the token out of the file by passing it through the environment:

export UV_INDEX_QPERFECT_USERNAME=__token__
export UV_INDEX_QPERFECT_PASSWORD=<your-access-token>
uv add mimiq-tensorweaver

To make the registry available everywhere instead, put the same table in ~/.config/uv/uv.toml as [[index]], without explicit = true (uv.toml has no sources table to pin a package with). The first-index rule then keeps the licensed wheel ahead of the mock.

The Qiskit integration is an optional extra:

pip install 'mimiq-tensorweaver[qiskit]'

So are the plots in tensorweaver.visualization, which need matplotlib:

pip install 'mimiq-tensorweaver[visualization]'

docs.title: Supported platforms
docs.text:
Wheels target Python's stable ABI, so one wheel per platform serves Python 3.11 and later. The free-threaded interpreter is served by a wheel of its own, since it has no stable ABI to target; see Free-threaded Python.

Platform Wheel tag Requires Linux x86_64 manylinux_2_35_x86_64 glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+); pulls the mkl runtime (~224 MB) Linux x86_64 manylinux_2_34_x86_64 glibc 2.34 (RHEL 9 and its rebuilds); pulls the mkl runtime (~224 MB) macOS arm64 macosx_26_0_arm64 macOS 26 or later, Apple Silicon Windows x86_64 win_amd64 Windows 10/11 x64; pulls the mkl runtime (~180 MB) Linux x86_64, python3.14t cp314-cp314t-manylinux_2_35_x86_64 glibc 2.35 or newer; free-threaded 3.14 only Linux x86_64, python3.14t cp314-cp314t-manylinux_2_34_x86_64 glibc 2.34 (RHEL 9 and its rebuilds); free-threaded 3.14 only

The mkl dependency is what makes linalg="mkl" work out of the box. MKL cannot be bundled into a wheel, so the wheels that have an MKL engine depend on it instead; see Linear-algebra engine. The Linux default engine is the vendored OpenBLAS and needs nothing.

Linux has two wheels, for glibc 2.35 and for glibc 2.34, because RHEL 9 ships 2.34. pip selects the one matching your host automatically. Check your version with ldd --version. Hosts below 2.34, such as RHEL 8 and Ubuntu 20.04, are not covered.

There are no wheels for Intel macOS or Linux aarch64. If pip reports no matching distribution, check this table first.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text:
The published wheel is licensed, and one binary serves both models. The license file decides at runtime which applies.

Model How it validates Node-locked Checks ~/.mimiq/license.key against the machine fingerprint, fully offline Floating Leases a short-lived seat from $QP_LICENSE_SERVER

Activate with the bundled qp-license CLI, also reachable as tensorweaver license:

tensorweaver license activate              # node-locked
tensorweaver license activate --floating   # floating

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
Source builds need a Rust toolchain, OpenBLAS + LAPACKE development packages, protoc, and SSH access to the QPerfect GitLab: Cargo fetches the Rust core, tensorweaver-rs, at the revision pinned in Cargo.toml.

git clone git@gitlab.qperfect.io:development/tensorweaver/tensorweaver-python.git
cd tensorweaver-python
scripts/dev-build.sh        # builds both BLAS engines into an editable install

To build against a local checkout of tensorweaver-rs instead, clone it next to tensorweaver-python and pass --config 'paths=["../tensorweaver-rs"]' to cargo or maturin.

maturin develop on its own builds only the MKL engine. That still runs, since the default engine follows the build, but it needs the MKL runtime on the system and gives you nothing to compare against, which is why dev-build.sh exists. See Linear-algebra engine for the runtime switch, and the repository README for build variants.

docs.title: Verify the install
docs.text:
python -c "import tensorweaver; print(tensorweaver.library_info())"

The documentation ships inside the wheel, with nothing loaded from the network, so it works on a machine that has none. Read it with:

tensorweaver docs

That serves the site on a free loopback port and opens a browser on it, and keeps running until you interrupt it. Pass --port to pin the port, or --print-path to print where the files live instead of serving them.

docs.title: Your first circuit
docs.text:
Build the circuit with mimiqcircuits, run it with execute().

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX, Measure
from tensorweaver import execute

# A Bell pair: H on qubit 0, then CX from 0 to 1.
c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)
c.push(Measure(), 1, 1)

results = execute(c, nsamples=1000, bonddim=64, seed=42)

Two keywords carry most of the meaning:

  • nsamples is how many shots you want.
  • bonddim caps the bond dimension, which is the accuracy/cost dial. 64 is ample for a Bell pair; see Concepts for how to choose it, and Circuit Execution for every other keyword.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
execute() returns a MIMIQ QCSResults.

print(results.histogram())
# {bs"00": 511, bs"11": 489}

print(results.fidelities[0])
# 1.0 -- nothing was discarded to truncation

print(results.timings)
# {'compile': ..., 'apply': ..., 'sample': ..., 'total': ...}
  • histogram() counts each measured classical state. Roughly half 00 and half 11, with no 01 or 10, is the Bell correlation.
  • fidelities reports how much weight truncation discarded, one entry per evolution. 1.0 means none. Treat it as a screen rather than a certificate: reading the reported fidelity explains what it does and does not cover.
  • timings breaks wall-clock seconds into compile, apply, sample, and total.

Individual shots are in results.cstates:

for bs in results.cstates[:5]:
    print(list(bs))     # [0, 0] or [1, 1]

docs.title: Asking for amplitudes
docs.text:
Pass the bitstrings you want and read them back from results.amplitudes. The amplitudes are read at the end of the circuit, so leave the measurements out: a measured state has already collapsed.

from mimiqcircuits import BitString

bell = Circuit()
bell.push(GateH(), 0)
bell.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

bs00, bs11 = BitString([0, 0]), BitString([1, 1])
results = execute(bell, nsamples=1, bonddim=64, bitstrings=[bs00, bs11])

print(results.amplitudes[bs00])   # ~0.7071+0j
print(results.amplitudes[bs11])   # ~0.7071+0j

Qiskit users

TensorWeaver is little-endian by qubit index: bitstring position i is qubit i, so bs[0] is qubit 0. Qiskit puts the highest-indexed qubit on the left, so bitstrings from results.cstates, results.histogram(), and mps.sample_bitstring() appear reversed compared to Qiskit output. The same convention applies to any BitString you pass in.

docs.title: Plotting the bond structure
docs.text:
With the visualization extra, plotbonds shows the bond dimension and the entanglement entropy of every cut, with the bonds at the cap in red, and plotschmidt the Schmidt spectrum of one cut. BondWindow follows a state as you evolve it.

from tensorweaver.visualization import plotbonds

fig = plotbonds(state)   # state: a TwState, such as TwSimulator.evolvezerostate returns

See Visualization for how to read the plots and use the window.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Concepts for bond dimension, fidelity, and execution modes.
  • Circuit Execution for every execute() keyword.
  • Examples for runnable scripts bundled with the package.
  • Visualization to plot the bond structure, or watch it grow.
  • API Reference for the low-level MPS and MPO classes.

The examples ship inside the installed package:

import tensorweaver as tw
print(tw.examples_dir())

docs.title: MockTensorWeaver
docs.text:
MockTensorWeaver is TensorWeaver's interface with nothing behind it. It takes the same constructor and the same execute call as TwSimulator, refuses exactly what TwSimulator refuses, and returns a real QCSResults full of nothing: all-zero samples, zero amplitudes, fidelity 1.0.

It is for validating the data models, what a MIMIQ backend accepts and what it hands back, on a machine that has no licence. That is a common shape of acceptance test: a customer's CI checks that its circuits build, that its options are accepted, that its results parse and round-trip, and it has no interest in the physics and no wish to pay for an hour of simulation to get there.

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorweaver import MockTensorWeaver

sim = MockTensorWeaver(bonddim=64, algorithm="cmpo")

c = mc.Circuit()
c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(mc.Measure(), [0, 1], [0, 1])

res = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=42)

res.simulator        # 'MockTensorWeaver'
len(res.cstates)     # 1000, every one a real BitString
res.histogram()      # {bs"00": 1000}
res.saveproto("out.pb")

Swapping it for the real thing is a one-line change, because the two take the same arguments:

from tensorweaver import TwSimulator as Sim      # licensed
from tensorweaver import MockTensorWeaver as Sim # unlicensed CI

docs.title: What it guarantees
docs.text:
It subclasses TwSimulator and overrides only the places where physics would happen: _evolve_circuit (the chokepoint every evolution route runs through), build_state, evolve, expectation and the three runtime-loss driver hooks. Everything that defines the interface is inherited, so the two cannot drift apart:

  • the constructor, with all its keywords and all its ValueError and TypeError checks: an algorithm TensorWeaver rejects is rejected here;
  • capabilities(), the same seventeen tokens, so the anti-capability sweep every MIMIQ backend runs gives identical verdicts;
  • limits(), topology(), can_handle(), default_passes();
  • execute(), with all its keywords, its seed/rng TypeError, its layout search for reorderqubits, and its NotImplementedError on the server-side remove_swaps;
  • the whole LocalBackend execution driver, which decides between the sampling and trajectory routes from the circuit, runs the pass pipeline, and builds the QCSResults itself.

tests/test_mock.py asserts those methods are not overridden (parity holds because they are inherited, so comparing their signatures would compare a function with itself), and separately records the expected argument names, so a knob added to one and not the other fails in CI rather than on a customer's machine.

What it does not do is compute. It is not a fast approximation, a low-fidelity mode, or a small-bond-dimension shortcut. Nothing is simulated.

docs.title: The public wheel
docs.text:
MockTensorWeaver is in every build, licensed or not, so one test suite can be run against both. It is also the only backend in the wheel published on public PyPI:

pip install mimiq-tensorweaver

No token, no index URL, no licence file. That wheel is the only one built with --features no-kernels: gate application on the MPS and the MPO, MPO application, compression and its truncation rule, the quantum channels and sampling are not in the binary in any form, having been kept from the compiler by #[cfg] rather than stripped afterwards. TwSimulator refuses to construct there and says so.

What the public wheel does carry is the MPS itself. MPS and MPO are the same native types, with their constructors, site tensors, bond dimensions, canonical form (the QR/LQ sweeps, which truncate nothing), norms, amplitudes, overlaps and serialization:

import tensorweaver as tw

tw.has_kernels()                 # False on the public wheel, True on a licensed one

mps = tw.MPS.zero_state(6, 32)
mps.recanonicalize(0)
mps.all_bond_dims()              # [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
mps.overlap(mps)                 # 1.0
tw.MPS.deserialize(mps.serialize())

mps.von_neumann_entropy(2)       # entanglement of a cut, in nats

mps.apply_gate_1q(...)           # AttributeError: the method is not there

docs.title: Measuring entanglement
docs.text:
The Schmidt spectrum of a cut is a property of the state, not a step in evolving one, so the entanglement read-outs are in every build:

mps = tw.MPS.deserialize(open("state.pb", "rb").read())

mps.schmidt_values(2)        # the spectrum of the cut at bond 2
mps.schmidt_rank(2, 1e-12)   # how many values clear a cutoff
mps.von_neumann_entropy(2)   # -Σ p ln p over the squared values, in nats
mps.all_entropies()          # every interior cut at once
tw.operator_entanglement(cx) # and the same measure for a gate, in bits

examples/00_mps_structure prints a state's whole entropy profile cut by cut, against the ceiling each cut's bond dimension allows, which is how you judge whether a run's bonddim was binding. Note the diagnostic is one-sided: a cut below its allocation is definitely not limited, but a cut that fills its allocation may be either truncated or exactly representable: GHZ fills χ=2 at every cut and loses nothing.

They go through a values-only singular-value routine that never returns the factors a truncation would need; choosing what to discard is the compression policy and stays in the licensed build. So an unlicensed install can open a state a licensed run produced and read its entanglement structure (where the correlations are, how much bond dimension each cut is really using) without being able to evolve it.

docs.title: Saving and loading states
docs.text:
MPS.serialize() and MPS.deserialize() are protobuf, and the conversion module is in every build. So a state evolved on a licensed machine can be opened on an unlicensed one:

# on the licensed machine
state, _ = sim.evolvezerostate(circuit)
open("state.pb", "wb").write(state.mps.serialize())

# anywhere, with a plain pip install and no licence
mps = tw.MPS.deserialize(open("state.pb", "rb").read())
mps.num_qubits, mps.all_bond_dims(), mps.amplitude([0] * mps.num_qubits)

It comes back as a live MPS, not a frozen record: canonicalise it, read its tensors, write to them, save it again. The same holds for MPO. What the unlicensed build cannot do with a loaded state is evolve it further.

The schema is proto/mpssim.proto in tensorweaver-rs, so the bytes are ordinary protobuf and any implementation can read them. tests/test_mock.py keeps fixtures produced by a licensed build and loads them on whatever build is installed, so the wire format cannot change under a customer's archive without a test failing.

The API is bytes in and bytes out; there is no file-level helper, and the MPSSim interop format (serialize_mpssim) is not exposed to Python in either build.

compile_info() reports the enabled build features, kernels among them, so a support report says which wheel is installed without anyone having to guess.

docs.title: Which wheel am I running?
docs.text:
The two distributions share a name and a version number, which is what lets pip install mimiq-tensorweaver work both with and without the QPerfect registry configured. They are told apart at runtime:

public PyPI QPerfect registry tw.has_kernels() False True TwSimulator() raises TensorWeaverError works MockTensorWeaver() works works licence required none node-locked or floating

Install the licensed wheel with an exclusive --index-url, as Getting started shows, not --extra-index-url: with both indexes in play, pip is free to prefer either copy of a name it finds in both.

docs.title: MIMIQ TensorWeaver: unlicensed mock
docs.text:
This distribution on PyPI is not the TensorWeaver simulator. It is MockTensorWeaver: the same interface, the same arguments, the same MIMIQ data models, and no simulation behind them. Results come back well-formed and empty: all-zero samples, zero amplitudes, fidelity 1.0.

It exists so that code which drives a MIMIQ backend can be tested on a machine with no licence: a CI job can check that its circuits build, that its options are accepted, that its results parse and round-trip, without paying for a simulation it does not care about.

pip install mimiq-tensorweaver

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorweaver import MockTensorWeaver

sim = MockTensorWeaver(bonddim=64)

c = mc.Circuit()
c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(mc.Measure(), [0, 1], [0, 1])

res = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=42)
res.histogram()        # {bs"00": 1000}: a real QCSResults, carrying nothing

MockTensorWeaver takes the same constructor and execute arguments as the licensed TwSimulator and refuses exactly what it refuses, so a configuration that fails here fails there. Swapping between them is an import change.

docs.title: What this build can and cannot do
docs.text:
It is compiled without the compute kernels. Gate application on the MPS and the MPO, MPO application, compression, the quantum channels and sampling are not in the binary.

What is here is the Matrix Product State itself, and it is the real one:

import tensorweaver as tw

tw.has_kernels()                 # False in this build

mps = tw.MPS.zero_state(8, 32)
mps.recanonicalize(0)            # canonical form, exact QR/LQ sweeps
mps.all_bond_dims()
mps.amplitude([0] * 8)
mps.von_neumann_entropy(2)       # entanglement of a cut, in nats
tw.MPS.deserialize(mps.serialize())

So a state produced by a licensed run can be saved, opened here, inspected, and have its entanglement structure read, without being able to evolve it further. tensorweaver.examples_dir() holds runnable examples; 00_mps_structure and 00_mock_backend work in this build, and the rest show what the licensed one does.

TwSimulator raises on construction here and says so.

docs.title: The licensed simulator
docs.text:
TensorWeaver is a Matrix Product State quantum circuit simulator for MIMIQ, distributed by QPerfect to licence holders from its own package registry rather than from PyPI.

For access, documentation and support: https://qperfect.io

docs.title: Qiskit integration
docs.text:
The optional tensorweaver.qiskit module runs Qiskit circuits on the MPS engine. A QuantumCircuit is converted to a mimiq circuit and evolved, so your Qiskit code stays unchanged.

Install the extra:

pip install 'mimiq-tensorweaver[qiskit]'

Bit ordering

Qiskit's own convention applies to Qiskit objects: counts keys come back with the highest-indexed qubit on the left, the reverse of the little-endian ordering TensorWeaver uses natively. The conversion handles this, so read Qiskit results as Qiskit results.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
TensorWeaverBackend is a Qiskit BackendV2. Simulator options (bonddim, seed, algorithm, and the rest of the TwSimulator configuration) are fixed when the backend is built. run takes shots and seed, and the circuit-preparation options of TwSimulator.execute: reorderqubits, fuse, fuse_threshold and canonicaldecompose, as in backend.run(qc, shots=4000, reorderqubits=True).

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from tensorweaver.qiskit import TensorWeaverBackend

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

backend = TensorWeaverBackend(bonddim=64, seed=1)
counts = backend.run(qc, shots=4000).result().get_counts()

It also works under Qiskit's V2 primitives:

from qiskit.primitives import BackendSamplerV2

sampler = BackendSamplerV2(backend=backend)
result = sampler.run([qc], shots=4000).result()[0]
counts = result.data.meas.get_counts()

docs.title: Expectation values
docs.text:
TensorWeaverEstimator is an EstimatorV2. Every Pauli term is read exactly from the MPS, whatever its weight, so there is no shot noise and the reported standard errors are zero. The only error is the MPS truncation itself, set by bonddim and the other simulator options, and reported as min_fidelity in the result metadata.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from tensorweaver.qiskit import TensorWeaverEstimator

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.ry(0.7, 2)

obs = SparsePauliOp.from_list([("ZZI", 1.0), ("IIZ", 0.5), ("ZZZ", 0.25)])

estimator = TensorWeaverEstimator(bonddim=64)
result = estimator.run([(qc, obs)]).result()[0]
print(result.data.evs, result.data.stds)

An estimator pub carries state preparation, not readout, so a measurement left at the end of the circuit is dropped rather than collapsing the state the observable is read from.

docs.title: Circuits that end in an ensemble
docs.text:
That exactness needs the circuit to end in one definite state. A mid-circuit measurement, a reset, a noise channel, or qubit loss makes TensorWeaver re-evolve the circuit once per shot, and each trajectory has its own expectation value. The quantity you want, Tr(rho O), is their average, so the estimator needs a budget to estimate it:

Argument What it does trajectories=N Average N trajectories. Each contributes an exact value, so only the ensemble is sampled. stds is the standard error of the mean. shots=N Estimate from measurements in rotated Pauli bases, N shots per basis, as hardware and Qiskit's BackendEstimatorV2 do. Terms that commute qubit-wise share a basis, so an observable needing several costs N shots in each. precision=p Size either budget as ceil(1/p**2), Qiskit's convention. method=... Force "exact", "trajectories", or "shots" instead of letting "auto" choose from the circuit. 
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)   # state preparation, not readout: the x follows it
qc.x(0)

obs = SparsePauliOp("Z")   # -1 or +1 per trajectory, 0 over the ensemble

averaged = TensorWeaverEstimator(trajectories=4000, seed=1)
result = averaged.run([(qc, obs)]).result()[0]
print(result.data.evs, "+/-", result.data.stds)

sampled = TensorWeaverEstimator(shots=4000, seed=1)   # the same quantity

Given no budget, a stochastic circuit raises rather than returning one trajectory as though it were exact. method="exact" forces that single-trajectory read anyway, with a warning: it is an unbiased draw, but its spread is the observable's own range, not a small error.

For the same budget, averaging trajectories is never worse than sampling and is usually better, because sampling adds the observable's shot noise on top of the ensemble's, and it runs one basis rather than several. Reach for shots= when you need to reproduce what a shot-based estimator would report, not for accuracy.

docs.title: Reading the metadata
docs.text:
{'target_precision': 0.0,
 'method': 'trajectories',   # or 'exact', 'shots'
 'exact': False,             # True only with no statistical error at all
 'stochastic': True,         # one evolution per shot was needed
 'trajectories': 4000,       # or 'shots': N
 'min_fidelity': 0.998}      # lowest MPS fidelity behind the pub

min_fidelity is the truncation error, not a statistical one. Averaging more trajectories does not improve it; raising bonddim does.

precision and default_precision do not change an exact value: a deterministic circuit has one answer and no shot budget to spend on it. To see plausible shot noise on such a circuit without paying for it, emulate_shot_noise=True adds Gaussian noise of width precision to the exact value, the way Qiskit's StatevectorEstimator does, for the cost of one evolution.

To reuse a configured simulator across both interfaces, pass it in rather than repeating the options:

from tensorweaver import TwSimulator
from tensorweaver.qiskit import TensorWeaverEstimator

sim = TwSimulator(bonddim=128, algorithm="vmpoa")
estimator = TensorWeaverEstimator(simulator=sim)

reorderqubits= on the estimator applies qubit reordering to every circuit it runs, as TwSimulator.execute(reorderqubits=...) does; see Qubit ordering.

docs.title: Gate coverage
docs.text: Conversion covers the standard Qiskit gate set. Custom gates and gates with unbound parameters raise mimiq_qiskit.converter.UnsupportedGateError: bind the parameters and decompose custom gates before running.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
tensorweaver.visualization draws the entanglement structure of an MPS: how large each bond has grown, how much entanglement each cut carries, and what the bond dimension cap cut off. It can also keep a window open that follows a state while you evolve it:

  • plotbonds plots the bond dimension and the entanglement entropy of every cut.
  • plotschmidt plots the Schmidt spectrum of one cut.
  • BondWindow is a window that moves gradually to the new bond structure each time you call update().

They answer the question that decides whether an MPS run can be trusted: is the bond dimension large enough for this circuit, and if not, where does it fall short? See Cutoffs and bond dimension for the knobs involved.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The plots need matplotlib, which the base install leaves out. The visualization extra adds it:

pip install 'mimiq-tensorweaver[visualization]'

The extra installs mimiqcircuits[visualization], so the plots use the same matplotlib version range and the same MIMIQ style as mimiqcircuits.visualization.plothistogram. import tensorweaver alone never loads matplotlib; the module is imported only when you ask for it:

from tensorweaver.visualization import plotbonds, plotschmidt, BondWindow

A BondWindow also needs a GUI toolkit for matplotlib to draw into; see Windows and backends. The two plots do not.

Every function takes a TwState, such as the one TwSimulator.evolvezerostate returns, or a bare MPS.

docs.title: Bond numbering
docs.text:
The plots number bonds as MPS.bond_dim and MPS.schmidt_values do: bond k is the cut between qubits k-1 and k. An n-qubit chain has interior bonds 1 to n-1; bonds 0 and n are its open ends, always of dimension 1, and are not drawn.

MPS.all_entropies() counts the other way, its element k being the cut between qubits k and k+1. The plots take care of the offset, so the entropy drawn at bond k is always that of the cut between k-1 and k.

docs.title: Bond dimensions and entropies: plotbonds
docs.text:
import mimiqcircuits as mc
import tensorweaver as tw
from tensorweaver.visualization import plotbonds

# A 12-qubit brickwork: RY rotations, then CX bricks on alternating pairs.
# Six layers entangle the middle of the chain more than χ = 4 can hold.
c = mc.Circuit()
for layer in range(6):
    for q in range(12):
        c.push(mc.GateRY(0.5 + 0.1 * q), q)
    for q in range(layer % 2, 11, 2):
        c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)

state, fidelity = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=4, strict_bonddim=False).evolvezerostate(c)
print(fidelity)                      # 0.9954...: truncation discarded some weight

fig = plotbonds(state)
fig.savefig("bonds.png")

docs.title: Reading the plot
docs.text:
Top panel: bond dimension χ. One bar per bond, on a log-2 axis, since bond dimensions grow by doublings: χ = 2 and χ = 256 both stay readable. The dashed line is max_bond_dim, the cap set by TwSimulator(bonddim=...).

  • A red bar has reached the cap. It holds as many Schmidt values as the simulator allows, so any further weight on that cut was discarded. Red marks where truncation can happen, not where it did: a state can fit its cap exactly, as a GHZ state does at χ = 2, and then nothing is lost. The fidelity returned with the state, and plotschmidt, tell how much it cost.
  • A bar below the cap was not limited by bonddim, though sv_cutoff can still have dropped small Schmidt values there.
  • χ = 1 means the two sides of the cut are not entangled at all.
  • Near the ends of the chain χ is bounded by the chain itself: bond k can never exceed 2**min(k, n-k) for qubits.

The title gives the largest χ in use and how many bonds sit at the cap. Several bonds at the cap and a fidelity below 1 mean the run needs a larger bonddim.

Bottom panel: entanglement entropy S. The von Neumann entropy of each cut, in nats: S = -Σ λᵢ² ln λᵢ² over the Schmidt values λᵢ. Zero is a product cut. One Bell pair across a cut gives ln 2 ≈ 0.693, and a cut of χ Schmidt values carries at most ln χ. The entropy says how much entanglement a bond carries, where χ only says how much room it takes.

docs.title: The spectrum of one cut: plotschmidt
docs.text:
from tensorweaver.visualization import plotschmidt

# Bond 6, the middle of the chain above, is at the cap.
fig = plotschmidt(state, 6)
fig.savefig("bond6.png")

Each bar is a Schmidt weight λᵢ², the probability carried by one Schmidt vector of the cut, largest first, on a log scale. The weights of a normalized state add up to 1. The title repeats χ and the entropy of the cut.

  • A spectrum that falls off fast, as here, means the cut is well represented: the smallest weight kept is about 10⁻³, so what the cap cut off beyond it was small.
  • A spectrum still high where it ends means the cap is cutting off weight that matters, and a larger bonddim would change the result.

Reading the spectrum moves the MPS orthogonality center to bond. That changes the MPS gauge, not the state: no amplitude changes.

docs.title: In notebooks and scripts
docs.text:
plotbonds and plotschmidt return a matplotlib.figure.Figure.

  • In a notebook, a call on the last line of a cell displays the figure once. Assigned to a variable (fig = plotbonds(state)), it displays nothing until you show fig.
  • In a script, save it with fig.savefig(...), or open it with matplotlib.pyplot.show().

Both take mimiqstyle=True by default; mimiqstyle=False draws in your active matplotlib style instead.

docs.title: Watching the bonds grow: BondWindow
docs.text:
BondWindow opens a window on a state and redraws it only when you call update(). Each update reads the state as it is then, and moves the picture there gradually over about a second. Between two updates you evolve the state by as many gates as you like, so you choose when to look.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mimiqcircuits as mc
import tensorweaver as tw
from tensorweaver.visualization import BondWindow

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=16, strict_bonddim=False)
state = sim.build_state(20)          # |0...0>: every bond at χ = 1
window = BondWindow(state)

# One layer: an RY on every qubit, then a CX ladder. Compile it once.
layer = mc.Circuit()
for q in range(20):
    layer.push(mc.GateRY(0.7), q)
for q in range(19):
    layer.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)
step = sim.compile(layer)

for _ in range(6):
    sim.evolve(state, step)          # evolve in place, any number of gates...
    window.update()                  # ...then animate to where the state is now

plt.show()                           # keep the window open at the end

TwSimulator.build_state(n) gives a fresh |0…0⟩ state, and TwSimulator.evolve(state, compiled) evolves it in place by a circuit that TwSimulator.compile prepared. The window keeps a reference to state and reads it at every update().

docs.title: What an update animates
docs.text:
The window shows what plotbonds shows. During an update:

  • bond dimensions move to their new values along the log-2 axis, so a bond going from 2 to 8 passes through 4 half way;
  • bars fade to red as they reach the cap, and back if they leave it;
  • entropies and the entropy axis move to their new values;
  • the title changes to the new state at the end.

The animation follows the clock: if the window redraws slowly it shows fewer frames, but still takes the time asked for.

docs.title: update()
docs.text:
window.update()                      # animate over the window's duration
window.update(duration=0.3)          # a quicker transition
window.update(duration=0)            # jump straight to the new picture

update() always reads the state the window was created on. To watch another state, open another window.

Argument Default Effect duration the window's Length of the animation in seconds; 0 jumps straight to the new picture.

BondWindow(state, mimiqstyle=True, duration=1.0) takes the same mimiqstyle as plotbonds, and duration sets the default length of an update.

update() raises RuntimeError once the window has been closed; open a new BondWindow to continue.

docs.title: Windows and backends
docs.text:
A window needs an interactive matplotlib backend, which in turn needs a GUI toolkit installed. The toolkit belongs to your environment, so the visualization extra does not install one:

  • Tk comes with most Python installs (python.org, Windows, conda, most Linux distributions), and matplotlib uses it with no setup.
  • Qt works with pip install PyQt6 or pip install PySide6. Use it where Python was built without Tk, as Homebrew's is.

Where the window is drawn from matters:

  • In a script, the window repaints only while update() runs. Between two updates it shows the last frame but does not respond to resizing. End the script with plt.show() to keep the window open and responsive, or pause with plt.pause(seconds) between updates.
  • In Jupyter, run %matplotlib qt (or %matplotlib tk) before creating the window. The notebook's default inline backend draws static images, which cannot animate.
  • With a non-interactive backend (Agg, inline), nothing opens and update() redraws the figure in one step. Nothing fails, so the same code runs in tests and on headless machines.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
The plots read little of the state. Bond dimensions are read directly. The entropies move the orthogonality center along the chain once, taking one SVD of a single site tensor per bond, and plotschmidt does the same for one cut. The MPS is never copied as a whole. A BondWindow makes the same reads at every update(), and none in between.

A state from a TwSimulator(usegpu=True) is brought back to host memory before it is read, as for any other read-out of the state.

docs.title: Tuning a run
docs.text:
An MPS simulation is an approximation you steer. The state is stored as a chain of tensors joined by bonds, and the width of those bonds is what a run pays for in memory and time. Every setting on this page is, in the end, about the same question: how much of the state do you keep, and how carefully do you choose what to drop.

There are three families of control, and they act at different points in a run.

Family Settings What it decides How much you keep bonddim, sv_cutoff, mpo_cutoff, entdim The ceiling on the state's width, and the thresholds below which weight is discarded. How the operator is applied algorithm How the simulator chooses which weight to drop when the ceiling binds. How the problem is laid out reorderqubits Where the entanglement sits on the chain in the first place.

Threads are a separate question: they change how fast a run goes, not what it computes. See Threads for the two pools and the variables that size them.

docs.title: The order to reach for them
docs.text:
Start with the layout. Reordering changes nothing physical and costs one pass over the gate list, but on a circuit whose interacting qubits are numbered far apart it can lower the bond dimension the run needs at all. It is the only control here that can make a problem cheaper without making it less accurate.

Then set the ceiling. bonddim is the main dial. Raise it until the observable you care about stops moving; that sweep, not any single number the run reports, is what tells you the answer has converged.

Then pick the algorithm, if the ceiling binds. While the state fits under bonddim, every algorithm is exact and the choice is only about speed. Once it does not fit, weight has to be discarded, and the algorithms differ in how well they choose. That is the point at which the choice starts to matter.

Leave the cutoffs alone unless you have a reason. sv_cutoff and mpo_cutoff are already set well below where they normally bind. They are worth touching when you need tighter accuracy at a bonddim you are not saturating, or when you want to trade accuracy for speed deliberately.

docs.title: How to tell which control is the one biting
docs.text:
Three symptoms, and what each points at.

The state sits at the ceiling. If the largest bond in use equals bonddim, truncation is happening on every application and accuracy is being paid away. Raise bonddim, improve the layout, or move to an algorithm that chooses its truncations more carefully.

import tensorweaver as tw

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=64)
state = sim.evolve(sim.zerostate(n), sim.compile(circuit))[0]
print(state.mps.max_used_bond_dim, "of", 64)

The state stays well below the ceiling. Raising bonddim buys nothing. If the result is still wrong, the limit is elsewhere: a cutoff, or a genuine bug.

The reported fidelity looks healthy but the answer moves. The fidelity accounts for discarded weight and nothing else. Treat it as a screen, not a certificate, and confirm with a bonddim sweep or a mirror circuit. See Reading the reported fidelity.

docs.title: What none of these can fix
docs.text: A circuit whose entanglement genuinely grows with depth will exceed any ceiling you can afford, on any setting. No layout hides all-to-all interaction, and no algorithm keeps weight that was never affordable to keep. When a bonddim sweep shows the observable still moving at the largest bonddim that fits in memory, the honest conclusion is that the circuit is beyond the method, not that the settings need more tuning.

docs.title: Choosing an algorithm
docs.text:
A circuit is applied to the state in blocks: gates are fused into an operator, and the operator is applied in one call. algorithm selects how that application is carried out.

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=128, algorithm="vmpoa")

All the algorithms compute the same product. They represent it exactly when the state fits under bonddim, and they differ only in how much of it survives when it does not. So the first thing to establish is whether the ceiling binds at all: if it does not, pick on speed alone.

The names say what each one is. The letter is the method and mpo is what it applies:

Setting Stands for "dmpo" direct MPO application "cmpo" canonical MPO application "vmpoa" variational MPO application, variant a "vmpob" variational MPO application, variant b

A second setting, strict_bonddim, decides whether the bonds may grow past bonddim while the operator is being applied. Each algorithm has its own default for it, and the defaults keep memory bounded by bonddim. See Strict and relaxed bond dimension below.

docs.title: The four
docs.text:
"dmpo", direct MPO application, applies the operator in a single pass over the chain, the zip-up. It is the cheapest per application. By default it cuts its intermediate to bonddim as it goes, like the reference MPS engine's zip-up, so its memory stays where bonddim puts it.

"cmpo", canonical MPO application, also applies the operator in a single pass, arranged so that the weight it discards is chosen against the state's own Schmidt spectrum. The name is the distinction: the truncation happens in canonical form, which is what makes those Schmidt values the right measure. It costs about what "dmpo" costs. When the ceiling binds it keeps more of the state, and it tends to leave the state narrower afterwards, which makes the gates that follow cheaper as well. It is also the accurate choice on GPU.

"vmpoa", variational MPO application variant a and the default, refines the result with single-site variational sweeps. It is the most accurate at a given bonddim on operators with long-range structure, and it costs roughly twice a single pass. It is the default because accuracy at a fixed bonddim is usually worth more than throughput: if a cheaper algorithm forces you to raise bonddim to recover the same fidelity, it was not the cheaper option.

"vmpob", variant b, refines with two-site sweeps. It converges best of the four and does the most work per sweep. Unlike the single-site variant it can widen a bond during refinement, which matters when the initial guess is too narrow to represent the answer.

docs.title: Strict and relaxed bond dimension
docs.text:
bonddim caps the bond dimension of the state you get back. While an operator is being applied, though, the algorithm works with intermediates that are wider than the result. strict_bonddim decides whether those intermediates are held to bonddim too.

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=64, algorithm="dmpo", strict_bonddim=False)

Strict (strict_bonddim=True) keeps every intermediate bond at or below bonddim. The zip-up cuts its carry to bonddim as it sweeps, so the memory a run needs follows from bonddim alone and you can size a machine by it. The price is where those cuts happen: in a gauge where the singular values are not the state's Schmidt values. A cut there can drop weight the exact result did not need to lose. The fidelity the run reports includes that loss, so a strict run is less accurate, not silently wrong.

Relaxed (strict_bonddim=False) lets the zip-up's carry grow to max(4 * bonddim, D), where D is the bond dimension of the operator, and then cuts to bonddim in canonical form, where the singular values are the right ones to compare. The result is exact whenever it fits under bonddim, whatever entdim is. It costs more memory and 1.5 to 4 times the time.

Either way the state you get back has no bond above bonddim.

docs.title: The defaults
docs.text:
Left at None, each algorithm takes its own default:

algorithm Default Strict Relaxed "dmpo" strict the zip-up cuts its carry to bonddim the carry grows to max(4 * bonddim, D) "vmpoa", "vmpob" strict the sweeps start from the strict zip-up the sweeps start from the relaxed zip-up "cmpo" relaxed not available: ValueError its sketch grows to 2 * bonddim

"cmpo" has no strict form. Its random sketch is up to twice bonddim wide, so its memory is still tied to bonddim, just not equal to it. Asking for algorithm="cmpo", strict_bonddim=True is refused when the simulator is built. A strict run also needs bonddim >= entdim; see Strict needs bonddim at least entdim.

For the variational algorithms the setting chooses the starting point of the sweeps. A single-site sweep ("vmpoa") cannot change a bond dimension, so it keeps the bond profile it starts from: on 20-qubit random circuits at bonddim 16 to 128, relaxed "vmpoa" reached 5 to 15% lower infidelity than strict, at 1.5 to 4 times the time. Two-site sweeps ("vmpob") adapt the bonds on their own, and relaxed "vmpob" matched strict to within 1% at 1.4 to 3 times the time.

docs.title: Strict needs bonddim at least entdim
docs.text:
A fused operator can reach bond dimension entdim (see entdim). Once the operator is wider than bonddim, a strict cut can do more than lose accuracy: it can wipe out the state altogether, driving even a state that is exactly a product state to zero norm.

So a run that resolves to strict with bonddim < entdim is refused with a ValueError when the simulator is built, before any circuit runs. The check uses entdim rather than the width each operator actually reaches, so whether a run is accepted does not depend on the circuit. To run it anyway:

  • Raise bonddim to entdim or above. With the defaults, bonddim=256 and entdim=16, the operator never outgrows the state.
  • Lower entdim to bonddim or below. Fewer gates fuse into each operator, so more applications run, each on a narrower operator.
  • Pass strict_bonddim=False, or use "cmpo", which is relaxed by default. Relaxed accepts any entdim at the cost in memory and time above.
import tensorweaver as tw

tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=4, entdim=16, algorithm="dmpo")   # ValueError
tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=4, entdim=16, algorithm="dmpo",
               strict_bonddim=False)                     # exact when it fits
tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=16, entdim=16, algorithm="dmpo")  # strict, accepted

The low-level MPS.apply_mpo makes the same check against the bond dimension of the operator it is given, and raises BondDimensionError.

docs.title: How much strict costs in accuracy
docs.text:
From entdim up, strict still cuts in the wrong gauge, and the cost depends on the algorithm:

  • "dmpo" suffers most. With bonddim only a little above entdim, the strict zip-up loses weight as a matter of routine. Deferring the compression sweep (post_compress=False) makes it worse.
  • The variational algorithms repair most of it. Their sweeps start from the strict zip-up and then optimise the result, so most of what the seed got wrong is recovered.

The fidelity a strict run reports includes what it lost. It can overestimate a fidelity that is already low, so read a low reported fidelity as "this run is not accurate" rather than as a precise figure. When it is too low, raise bonddim or pass strict_bonddim=False.

A high reported fidelity is still not proof of convergence. Check it as described in Deciding it by measurement.

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
• Choose strict (the default for "dmpo", "vmpoa", "vmpob") when memory has to be predictable from bonddim: a shared machine, a large bonddim close to what fits, or a batch of runs sized in advance. Watch the reported fidelity, which shows what it cost.
  • Choose relaxed when memory has headroom and accuracy at a given bonddim matters more than time: a small bonddim, an entdim above bonddim (where strict is refused), or a circuit whose state you expect to stay narrow and want exactly.
  • If you want relaxed behaviour at single-pass cost, "cmpo" already runs that way.

docs.title: Picking one
docs.text: Situation Reach for The state stays well below bonddim "cmpo", or "dmpo" with strict_bonddim=False. Both are exact here, and both are single passes. A long run at a bonddim that binds "cmpo". Single-pass cost, and the narrower state it leaves compounds over the run. Highest accuracy at a fixed bonddim "vmpoa", or "vmpob" where the operator has structure a single-site sweep converges poorly on. Reproducing a MIMIQ or MPSSim baseline "vmpoa", which starts from the same zip-up as MPSSim's default. A little more accuracy than "vmpoa", at a higher cost "vmpoa" with strict_bonddim=False. bonddim below entdim "cmpo", or any algorithm with strict_bonddim=False. Strict is refused here. usegpu=True "cmpo". See GPU engine. You are not sure Leave the default. Then sweep.

docs.title: Deciding it by measurement
docs.text:
The reliable way to choose is to run the same circuit both ways and compare the observable you actually care about, not the reported fidelity.

import tensorweaver as tw

for algorithm in ("dmpo", "cmpo", "vmpoa"):
    sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=64, algorithm=algorithm, seed=1)
    state, fidelity = sim.evolve(sim.zerostate(n), sim.compile(circuit))
    print(f"{algorithm:>6}  chi {state.mps.max_used_bond_dim:>4}  "
          f"fidelity {fidelity.value:.6f}")

Two columns are worth reading, not one.

The fidelity says how much weight each algorithm kept. A larger number means less was discarded.

The final bond dimension says how wide the state it produced is. This is the column that is easy to overlook and often the more useful of the two: an algorithm that finishes narrower is not only more compact, it makes every subsequent gate cheaper, and the effect compounds across a long circuit. Two algorithms can report similar fidelities and leave states of very different width.

If the two algorithms give the same answer, take the cheaper. If they disagree, the ceiling is binding and the disagreement is telling you the run is not converged. Raise bonddim until they agree, and then decide on cost.

docs.title: On the GPU
docs.text: A state moved onto the device runs "dmpo" and "cmpo" there. The variational algorithms run on the host, and the simulator refuses them rather than transferring the state back and forth for every application, which would cost more than the refinement saves. Between the two that do run, prefer "cmpo".

docs.title: What the choice does not affect
docs.text: algorithm and strict_bonddim do not change the ceiling, the cutoffs, or the layout. It changes which weight is discarded once something has to be, and nothing else. If a run is inaccurate because bonddim is far too small for the circuit, no algorithm will rescue it; see Cutoffs and bond dimension.

docs.title: Cutoffs and bond dimension
docs.text:
Four settings decide how much of the state and of the operator a run keeps. They act at different stages, and the tightest one in play is what bounds a run's accuracy, so it is worth knowing which stage each belongs to.

Setting Default Acts on Kind bonddim 256 The state Hard ceiling on the bond dimension. sv_cutoff 1e-7 The state Threshold below which Schmidt values are discarded. mpo_cutoff 1e-15 The operator Threshold used while gates are fused into an operator. entdim 16 The operator Ceiling on the operator's own width. Not an accuracy dial; see below.

docs.title: bonddim, the ceiling
docs.text:
The bond dimension is how much entanglement the state can carry across a cut. bonddim caps it, and it is never exceeded. This is the main accuracy and cost control: memory grows with it, and the linear algebra that applies gates grows faster still, so doubling bonddim is considerably more than twice the work.

The ceiling is a hard cut. It discards weight whether or not the weight is small, which is what distinguishes it from the cutoffs below.

Whether it is binding is directly observable:

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=64)
state, fidelity = sim.evolve(sim.zerostate(n), sim.compile(circuit))
print(state.mps.max_used_bond_dim, "of", 64)

If that reads 64 of 64 the ceiling is binding and accuracy is being paid away on every application. If it reads 12 of 64, raising bonddim buys nothing at all and you can lower it to save memory.

docs.title: sv_cutoff, the state-side threshold
docs.text:
After each application the affected bonds are re-factored and Schmidt values below sv_cutoff are dropped, even when the bond is under the ceiling. It is an absolute threshold, not one relative to the largest value.

At the default of 1e-7 it removes weight that is numerically negligible for most work and usually costs nothing. Lower it toward 1e-10 when you need tighter accuracy at a bonddim you are not saturating, which is the regime where it, rather than the ceiling, is the binding control. Raise it to trade accuracy for speed deliberately.

docs.title: mpo_cutoff, the operator-side threshold
docs.text:
Gates are fused into an operator before being applied, and that fusion has its own truncation. mpo_cutoff is its threshold. It is independent of sv_cutoff, and it is set at 1e-15, effectively exact, so that the operator is not what limits a run.

That independence is the thing to understand about it. A loose mpo_cutoff caps a run's accuracy no matter how tight sv_cutoff and bonddim are, because the operator being applied is already an approximation of the circuit before the state ever sees it. Loosen it only when you have measured that intermediate operators are the memory problem, and expect a matching loss of accuracy.

docs.title: entdim, the operator's width
docs.text:
entdim caps the bond dimension of the operator that gates accumulate into. Gates keep fusing into one operator until the next would exceed it, at which point the operator is applied and a fresh one is started. Raising it batches more gates per application, which is usually faster on deep, strongly entangling segments; lowering it keeps intermediate operators small.

entdim is deliberately not an accuracy dial in the way the others are. A single gate whose operator rank exceeds entdim raises an error rather than being applied at reduced accuracy. Silently approximating a gate you asked for is not a trade the simulator makes on your behalf, so an entdim that is too small tells you so.

entdim also bounds how wide the operator applied to the state can be. With the default, strict bond dimension ("dmpo", "vmpoa", "vmpob"), an operator wider than bonddim can wipe out the state, so a strict run needs bonddim >= entdim and raises ValueError otherwise. Keep bonddim at or above entdim, or pass strict_bonddim=False, or use "cmpo". See Strict and relaxed bond dimension.

docs.title: How they interact
docs.text:
The four compose, and the tightest bound wins:

  • The operator is built subject to entdim and mpo_cutoff.
  • That operator is applied to the state, and the result is truncated subject to bonddim and sv_cutoff.

So an accurate run needs every stage to be accurate. Tightening sv_cutoff while leaving mpo_cutoff loose changes nothing, because the error is already in the operator.

docs.title: Establishing that a result is converged
docs.text:
No single number a run reports tells you the answer is right. The reported fidelity accounts for discarded weight and nothing else, so it is a screen rather than a certificate; see Reading the reported fidelity.

The convergence check is to vary the control that bounds the approximation and watch the observable you care about:

for chi in (16, 32, 64, 128, 256):
    results = tw.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, bonddim=chi, seed=1)
    print(chi, results.fidelities[0], results.histogram())

When the observable stops moving as bonddim grows, the answer is converged. When it is still moving at the largest bonddim you can afford, it is not, and the fidelity was not telling you the whole story.

A mirror circuit is the other standard check, and it is the stronger one because it tests the state rather than the bookkeeping: apply \(U\), then \(U^\dagger\), and measure how much of \(|0\dots0\rangle\) comes back.

Example 05 in the bundled examples runs a bonddim sweep against a high-bonddim reference.

docs.title: Deferred compression (post_compress)
docs.text:
post_compress is a cost control rather than an accuracy threshold, but it belongs here because turning it off changes what the cutoffs mean.

With it on, which is the default, a compression pass runs after every operator application and returns the state to canonical form. Canonical form is what makes the values compared against sv_cutoff the state's true Schmidt weights. With it off, that pass is deferred, so later truncations compare values that are no longer those weights, and the bond dimension can drift upward on numerical noise.

Leave it on unless you have measured that your circuits are unaffected.

docs.title: Qubit ordering
docs.text:
An MPS is a one-dimensional chain. Entanglement between neighbouring sites is cheap; entanglement between distant sites is expensive, because every bond in between has to carry it. A gate on qubits 0 and 40 forces a wide bond across everything separating them, and the cost is paid by every gate that follows.

Qubit numbering is a labelling, not physics. Relabelling so that interacting qubits sit near each other can lower the bond dimension a circuit needs, for the same answer. This is the one control that can make a run cheaper without making it less accurate.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Reordering is off by default. The layout you wrote is the layout that runs. It is a circuit-preparation pass, so you ask for it per run, not when you build the simulator:

import tensorweaver as tw

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=64)
results = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, reorderqubits=True)

True runs the whole portfolio of searches and keeps whichever result scores best. Naming one ("greedy", "sa" / "simulated_annealing", "multilevel") pins the search instead, which is mostly useful for comparing them: the result is scored the same way either way.

The free function takes the same flag:

results = tw.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, reorderqubits=True)

The flag runs TwReorderQubitsPass with its default settings. To set them, for example the margin described below, pass the pass yourself:

from mimiqcircuits.backends import PassPipeline

results = sim.execute(
    circuit, nsamples=1000,
    passes=PassPipeline([tw.TwReorderQubitsPass(margin=4.0)]),
)

docs.title: How a layout is chosen
docs.text:
The searches minimise the total weighted distance between interacting qubits. That is a good thing to descend, and a poor thing to decide by: it has no bond dimension in it, so it cannot tell a layout that fits under your cap from one that does not, and on a ring it will happily fold the chain and double every cut.

So the search result is not the answer, it is a candidate. What decides is a different cost. For each bond k of the chain, with u_k two-qubit gate applications crossing it and h_k bits of entanglement those gates can create:

C = Σ_k  u_k · max(0, min(h_k, k, n−k) − log2(bonddim))

Over every bond: how many truncations happen there, times how many bits each one has to throw away. C = 0 means no bond ever exceeds bonddim, so the layout truncates nothing. Your own layout is always one of the candidates, and a search result has to beat it by the pass's margin (default 2.0) before it is used. A layout that truncates nothing is used whatever the margin.

Two consequences worth knowing:

  • bonddim changes the answer. The same circuit can want different layouts at 64 and at 1024, because what matters is which bonds do not fit.
  • Gates are weighted by what they entangle, not by how many there are. A CP(π) is worth one bit, a CP(1e-9) none, so a cloud of negligible controlled phases does not drag the layout towards gates that do nothing.

docs.title: What it decided, and why
docs.text:
Both outcomes are reported, so you never have to guess whether the pass helped:

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=256)
sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, reorderqubits=True)
print(sim.last_layout_report)

The report carries the cost, the widest bond in bits, and the number of bonds over budget, each for the chosen layout and for the one you wrote, plus which search won. It is also logged at INFO on the tensorweaver.reorder logger:

import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

docs.title: You get your own labelling back
docs.text: The permutation is internal. Samples, amplitudes, and z-variables are all translated back to the qubit numbering you wrote, so nothing downstream has to know a reordering happened. A circuit run with and without reordering answers in the same frame.

docs.title: When it helps
docs.text:
Reordering pays when the interaction graph has locality that the numbering hides:

  • long-range pairings, such as a circuit coupling qubit i with qubit n-1-i
  • a layout inherited from hardware whose numbering does not match its connectivity
  • a circuit generated from a graph problem, where the graph is local but the labelling is arbitrary

It cannot help when the interaction graph is genuinely all-to-all, because there is no layout in which every pair is close. It does nothing for a circuit that is already nearest-neighbour, because the identity permutation is already the best one. In both cases the searches run, score no better than your layout, and the circuit passes through unchanged.

The search is a compile step, so it costs preparation time: milliseconds on a hundred qubits, under a second on a thousand. Above a size threshold the portfolio runs fewer searches rather than slower ones, so it never costs more than a large multiple of a single search.

docs.title: Deciding whether it is worth it
docs.text:
Measure it. The peak bond dimension is the number that moves:

import tensorweaver as tw

import mimiqcircuits as mc

sim = tw.TwSimulator(bonddim=256, seed=1)
for reorder in (False, True):
    # BondDim at the middle of the chain reports the width the run needed there.
    probe = mc.Circuit()
    for inst in circuit.instructions:
        probe.push(inst.operation, *inst.qubits, *inst.bits, *inst.zvars)
    probe.push(mc.BondDim(), n // 2, probe.num_zvars())
    res = sim.execute(probe, nsamples=1, reorderqubits=reorder)
    print(f"reorderqubits={reorder!s:>5}  "
          f"chi {int(res.zstates[0][-1].real):>4}  "
          f"fidelity {float(res.fidelities[0]):.6f}")

Run it once at a bonddim large enough that neither configuration saturates, so you are comparing the width each layout genuinely needs rather than the ceiling. If the reordered run needs a much smaller bond dimension, it will be faster and more accurate at every bonddim below that; if the two are close, the layout was already reasonable and reordering is not where the cost is.

Example 07 in the bundled examples builds the canonical bad case and prints the peak bond dimension with and without reordering.

docs.title: Bond observables pin the layout
docs.text:
Bond observables are the one thing not permuted. BondDim(), SchmidtRank() and VonNeumannEntropy() take a bond index, naming the bipartition {0..k-1} | {k..n-1}, not a qubit. A layout that moved a qubit across such a cut would change what the observable measures, so those cuts are kept intact and the index is left alone: the observable still reports the bipartition you asked for.

A circuit that profiles every bond is therefore fully pinned, and no reordering is available to it.

docs.title: Reading the entropy profile
docs.text: Where the entanglement sits is what tells you whether a different layout could help at all. The von Neumann entropy across each bond is the direct measurement: a profile with one tall peak in the middle usually means a few long-range couplings are responsible and a layout change may pay, while a broad, flat profile means the entanglement is spread across the whole chain and no relabelling will concentrate it.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: TensorWeaver runs on threads it does not create itself: the linear algebra runs on the threads of the BLAS or of faer, and sampling runs on a rayon pool. This page covers how many of each a run gets, how to change it, and how to check what a run actually used.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: You want Do One count for everything, for the whole process export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=8 before starting Python Different counts for evolution and sampling MIMIQ_CORE_NUM_THREADS and MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS A cap for the runs of one simulator TwSimulator(max_num_threads=4) To run inside a container or a batch allocation Set MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS to the CPUs you were given (see Containers and batch jobs) To see what a run resolved tensorweaver.thread_info()

docs.title: The two pools
docs.text:
Pool What runs on it Sized by core Linear algebra: gate application, compression, decompositions. MIMIQ_CORE_NUM_THREADS sampler Drawing shots from the evolved state. MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS

Both fall back to MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS when their own variable is unset. So the common case is one variable:

export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=8      # both pools, eight threads each

and the uncommon case is two:

export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=8          # eight by default
export MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS=2  # except sampling, which gets two

The pools scale differently, which is why they are separate. The core pool parallelises inside each tensor contraction, which pays off when the bond dimension is large and can cost more than it saves when it is small. The sampler pool parallelises across shots, which pays off whenever you ask for many shots, whatever the bond dimension. A circuit with a small bond dimension and ten thousand shots wants few core threads and many sampler threads; a deep circuit at bond dimension 512 sampled once wants the opposite.
